(p-423) Surah al-Ma'idah

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who have believed, fulfill the contracts.﴾ It is said: "wafa bil-'ahd" and "awfa bihi" (he fulfilled the pledge). The ʿaqd (contract) is a firm covenant. It is likened to the tying of a rope or the like. The contracts meant are either the contracts of Allah which He made with His servants and imposed upon them among the obligations of legal responsibility (taklif), or what Allah has contracted upon you and what you have contracted among yourselves. The apparent meaning is that they are the contracts of Allah upon them in His religion, concerning the making lawful of what He has made lawful and the making unlawful of what He has made unlawful. This is a statement presented in summary, then followed by detail, which is His saying: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle﴾. The word bahimah (beast) refers to every four-legged creature on land and sea. Its being attributed to al-an'am (cattle) is for explanation (bayan), and it carries the meaning of "min" (of), as in "a ring of silver" (khatim fiddah), and its meaning is: the beasts of the cattle, namely the eight pairs. It is also said: bahimat al-an'am refers to gazelles, wild cattle, and the like.

﴿Except what is recited to you﴾ refers to the verse of its prohibition, which is His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you is carrion﴾ up to the end of the verse. ﴿Not hunting while you are in the state of ihram﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "lakum" (for you); that is: these things are made lawful for you, not as those who make the hunt lawful.

﴿And you are in the state of ihram (hurum)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "muhilli al-sayd" (those who make hunting lawful); as if it was said: We have made lawful for you some of the cattle while you abstain from hunting and are in the state of ihram, so that it not be made difficult for you. The word hurum is the plural of haram, which means muhrim (one in the state of ihram).

﴿Indeed, Allah decrees what He wills﴾ of the rulings, or of making lawful and making unlawful.

(p-424)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 2:

It was revealed as a prohibition against making lawful what Allah has made unlawful: ﴿O you who believe, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾. "Sha'a'ir" is the plural of "sha'ira" (ritual marker), which is the name for that which is marked (ushʻira), meaning that which is made a sign and a mark of the rites of pilgrimage, such as the standing places of Hajj (mawaqif), the places where the pebbles are thrown (marami al-jimar), the Tawaf (circumambulation) area, the Sa'y (running between Safa and Marwa), and the acts that are the marks of the pilgrim, by which he is recognized: the ihram, the tawaf, the sa'y, the shaving of the head (halq), and the sacrifice (nahr).

﴿Nor the sacred month﴾, that is, the months of Hajj. ﴿Nor the hadi﴾, which is what is brought as a gift to the House and drawn near to Allah the Exalted by the pilgrims. It is the plural of "hadiyya" (gift).

﴿Nor the garlands﴾. "Qala'id" is the plural of "qala'ida" (garland), which is that with which the hadi is garlanded, whether a sandal, the handle of a water-skin, tree bark, or something else.

﴿Nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾. Do not make lawful a people intending the Sacred Mosque, namely the pilgrims (hujjaj) and the performers of the lesser pilgrimage ('umar). Making these things lawful means: treating the sanctity of the rites lightly; preventing them and those who observe them in worship from reaching them; creating, in the months of Hajj, things by which people are turned away from Hajj; and attacking the hadi by seizing it or preventing it from reaching its place of sacrifice. As for the "garlands", it is permissible that by them is meant the garlanded animals themselves, namely the camels (al-budn), and they are joined to the hadi for their distinction, since they are the noblest of the hadi, like His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers, and to Jibril and Mikail﴾ [al-Baqara: 98]; as if it were said: "and the garlands among them in particular." It is also permissible that He forbids touching the garlands of the hadi as an intensification of the prohibition against touching the hadi itself, meaning: do not make lawful their garlands, let alone make them lawful, just as He said: ﴿and not to reveal their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31], so He forbade revealing the adornment as an intensification of the prohibition against revealing its places.

﴿Seeking﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "aminin" (those coming). ﴿Bounty from their Lord﴾, that is, reward. ﴿And good pleasure﴾, and that He be pleased with them. Do not touch a people who have this description, as an honoring of them.

﴿And when you come out of the state of ihram (halaltum)﴾, that is, you leave the state of ihram. ﴿Then hunt﴾, as a permission for hunting after its prohibition upon them by His saying: ﴿not hunting game while you are in the state of ihram﴾.

﴿And let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress﴾. "Jarama" works like "kasaba" (to earn) in taking one object or two objects. You say: "jarama dhanban" (he committed a sin), like "kasabahu" (he earned it), and "jaramtuhu dhanban" (I caused him to earn a sin), like "kasabtuhu iyyahu". The first object is the pronoun of those addressed, and the second is "an ta'tadu" (that you transgress). And "an sadduukum" is connected to "shana'an" in the sense of cause, and it is intense hatred. With a sukun on the nun, it is read by al-Shami (one of the Qur'anic readers) and Abu Bakr. The meaning: let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you, earn you (the sin of) transgression, nor compel you to it. "In sadduukum" with the conditional (in) is read by Makki and Abu 'Amr. The meaning of their barring you from the Sacred Mosque is that the people of Makka prevented the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers from the 'umra on the day of al-Hudaybiyya. The meaning of "transgression" is retaliation against them by inflicting harm upon them.

﴿And help one another in righteousness and piety﴾, through pardon and overlooking. ﴿And do not help one another in sin and aggression﴾, through retaliation and taking revenge. Or: "birr" is doing what is commanded, "taqwa" is abandoning what is forbidden, "ithm" is abandoning what is commanded, and "udwan" is doing what is forbidden. It is also permissible that the meaning is general, covering every righteousness and piety, and every sin and aggression, so that by its generality it includes both pardon and retaliation.

﴿And fear Allah; indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys Him, and for whoever does not fear Him.

They ask you (﴿يَسْألُونَكَ﴾): the verb of asking carries the sense of saying, so what follows it is in the form of speech. Hence ﴿ماذا أُحِلَّ لَهُمْ﴾ ("What has been made lawful for them?") comes after it, as if it were said: "They say to you: ﴿What has been made lawful for them?﴾." He did not say "What is made lawful for us?" in reporting what they said, because ﴿يَسْألُونَكَ﴾ is in the third-person form (ghaybah), like your saying: "Zayd swore that he would do it" (aqsama Zaydun la-yafʿalanna), whereas if one said "I will do it" (la-afʿalanna) and "what is made lawful for us" (wa-uḥilla lana), it would also be correct. ﴿ماذا﴾ ("what") is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and ﴿أُحِلَّ لَهُمْ﴾ ("has been made lawful for them") is its predicate (khabar). This is like your saying: "What is made lawful for them?" Its meaning is: "What has been made lawful for them of foods?" It seems that when he recited to them what had been forbidden to them of foul foods, they asked what was lawful for them of them, and he said: ﴿Say: The good things have been made lawful for you﴾, i.e., what is not foul among them. Or it means: everything whose prohibition has not come in the Book of Allah, or the Sunnah, or consensus (ijma', the agreement of scholars), or analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy from a established ruling).

﴿وَما عَلَّمْتُمْ﴾ ("and what you have trained") is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿الطَيِّباتُ﴾ ("the good things"), meaning: ﴿the good things have been made lawful for you, and the game caught by what you have trained﴾, with an elided genitive (the word "hunting" or "game" has been omitted). Or you may make ﴿ما﴾ conditional (sharṭiyyah, a conditional particle), with its answer being ﴿فَكُلُوا﴾ ("then eat"). ﴿مِنَ الجَوارِحِ﴾ ("from the hunting animals", lit. "the trained ones that seize") means the predators that hunt game, from wild beasts and birds, such as the dog, the leopard, the eagle, the falcon, the hawk, and the shāhīn (a kind of falcon). It has been said that the word is derived from "wound" (jirāḥah), so that the lawfulness of the kill requires that it be wounded. ﴿مُكَلِّبِينَ﴾ ("training them") is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject or object) of ﴿عَلَّمْتُمْ﴾. The benefit of this circumstantial clause, though the meaning is already given by ﴿عَلَّمْتُمْ﴾, is that the one who trains the hunting animals should be described as a trainer (mukallib). The mukallib is the one who disciplines and teaches the hunting animals, derived from kalab (dog), because disciplining is most common among dogs, so the word was derived from their name because of its frequency in their category. Or because a predator is called a kalb (dog). From this comes the ḥadīth: "O Allah, set against him a dog from Your dogs," and then a lion devoured him.

﴿تُعَلِّمُونَهُنَّ﴾ ("you teach them") is a circumstantial clause, or a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf, a new independent sentence), and it has no grammatical position (lā mawḍiʿa lahu). In this there is evidence that everyone who takes up a knowledge should take it only from the most skilled of its people and the most expert in understanding it. How many a person who takes it from one not proficient has wasted his days, and bitten his fingertips at meeting the masters (naḥārīr)?!

﴿مِمّا عَلَّمَكُمُ اللهُ﴾ ("of what Allah has taught you") refers to training. ﴿فَكُلُوا مِمّا أمْسَكْنَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ ("then eat of what they catch for you"): holding on to the game for its owner means that it does not eat from it. If it eats from it, it is not to be eaten when it is game caught by a dog or the like. As for game caught by a falcon or the like, its eating from it does not make it unlawful, as is known in its proper place. The pronoun in ﴿واذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللهِ عَلَيْهِ﴾ ("and mention the name of Allah over it") refers to ﴿ما أمْسَكْنَ﴾ ("what they catch"), in the sense: pronounce the name over it if you reach it before its slaughter. Or it refers to ﴿ما عَلِمْتُمْ مِنَ الجَوارِحِ﴾ ("what you have trained of the hunting animals"), meaning: pronounce the name over it when you release it. ﴿واتَّقُوا اللهَ﴾ ("and fear Allah"): beware of violating His command in all of this. ﴿إنَّ اللهَ سَرِيعُ الحِسابِ﴾ ("indeed Allah is swift in reckoning"): He will call you to account for your actions, and no delay (labath) will reach Him in this.

(p-428)

﴿Today﴾, that is, now, ﴿the good things have been made lawful for you﴾. He repeated it to emphasise the favour (al-minnah). ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾, meaning their slaughtered animals (dhaba'ih), because the lawfulness of other foods is not restricted to one religious community. ﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾, so there is no blame on you if you feed them, because if the food of the believers were forbidden to them, it would not be permissible for them to feed them. ﴿And the chaste women from among the believing women﴾ are the free women (al-hara'ir), or the chaste ones (al-'afa'if). This is not a condition for the validity of marriage. It is a recommendation (li-l-istihbab), because marriage to Muslim slave women is valid, and marriage to women who are not chaste is valid. Specifying them is an urging on the believers to choose carefully for their offspring (nutaf). It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "the good things", or it is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: "and the chaste women from among the believing women are lawful for you". ﴿And the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ are the free women of the People of the Scripture, or the chaste women of the People of the Scripture.

﴿When you have given them their wages﴾, meaning you have given them their dowries (muhur), ﴿being chaste, not fornicating, and not taking secret lovers﴾. Being chaste means being married, not being adulterers (zaniyin). Akhdan means lovers, and al-khidn (a lover) applies to both male and female. ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith﴾, meaning in the laws of Islam and in what Allah has made lawful and what He has made unlawful, ﴿his deeds have become void﴾, meaning they have been nullified, ﴿and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verse 6:

﴿O you who believe, when you rise to the prayer, wash your faces﴾. That is: when you intend to rise to the prayer, as in His saying: ﴿When you recite the Qur'an﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], meaning: when you intend to recite the Qur'an. He expresses the intention to do an act by the act itself, because the act is caused by the intention, so the effect is put in the place of the cause, owing to the connection between them, for the sake of brevity. A similar example is "As you judge, so you will be judged" (*kama tadin tudan*), where the initiating act, which is the cause of the requital, is expressed by the word for the requital, which is its effect. Its implied sense is: "while you are in a state of *hadath*" (ritual impurity). From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: or [the implied meaning is] "from sleep," because it is an indication of *hadath*. "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Companions used to perform ablution for every prayer." It has been said that ablution for every prayer was obligatory at first when it was prescribed, then it was abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation).

﴿and your hands up to the elbows﴾. "Ila" (up to) indicates the meaning of a limit (*ghayah*) in an absolute sense. As for whether it is included in the ruling or excluded from it, this is a matter that depends on the evidence. Where there is evidence for exclusion, as in ﴿then [let there be] postponement until a time of ease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 280], since hardship is the reason for granting respite, and when ease is present the reason ceases; if the time of ease were included in it, the respite would be given in both states, the state of hardship and the state of ease. Likewise, ﴿Complete the fast until the night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]: if the night were included, then continuous fasting (*wisal*) would be obligatory. Among the examples where there is evidence for inclusion is your saying: "I memorized the Qur'an from its beginning to its end," because the speech is aimed at memorizing the entire Qur'an. From the same usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1], because it is known that the Prophet ﷺ was not taken by night to Bayt al-Maqdis without entering it. As for His saying ﴿to the elbows﴾, there is no evidence in it for either of the two matters. The majority (*al-jumhur*) took the cautious course and ruled that the elbows are included in the washing. Zufar and Dawud took the course of certainty and did not include them.

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that "he would pour water over his elbows."

﴿and wipe your heads﴾. The intended meaning is attaching the wiping to the head. Whether one wipes part of it or the whole of it, both have attached the wiping to the head. Malik took the cautious course and made the wiping of the whole head obligatory. Al-Shafi'i took the course of certainty and made obligatory the least amount to which the term "wiping" applies. We follow the Prophet's ﷺ explanation, which is what is reported: "that he wiped over his forelock (*nasiyah*)." The forelock was assessed as one quarter of the head.

(And your feet up to the ankles): read with the accusative by Ibn 'Amir of Syria (*Shami*), Nafi', 'Ali and Hafs. The meaning is: "wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and your feet up to the ankles, and wipe your heads," with inversion of order (*taqdim wa ta'khir*). Others read it in the genitive, by coordination with "heads." Because the feet, among the three washed limbs, are washed by pouring water over them, they were liable to excess (*israf*), which is forbidden. So they were coordinated with the wiped part, not so that they would be wiped, but to draw attention to the obligation of moderation in pouring water over them. It has also been said: "up to the ankles" was mentioned with the limit so as to dispel the suspicion of someone who might think they are to be wiped, since no limit is set for wiping in the Law.

In *Jami' al-'Ulum*, it is said that they are in the genitive by proximity (*li'l-jiwar*). It is authentically related that "the Prophet ﷺ saw some people wiping over their feet, and he said: 'Woe to the heels from the Fire.'"

It is related from 'Ata': "By Allah, I do not know that any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wiped over the two feet." The washing of these limbs was only commanded so that they might be purified from the dirt that clings to them, because they are often exposed. And prayer is the service of Allah, exalted is He, and standing before Him purified from dirt is closer to honouring Him, and so it is more complete in service, as in the case of a witness who wishes to stand before a king. For this reason it has been said that it is preferable for a man to pray in his best clothes, and that praying while wearing a turban is better than praying with the head uncovered, because that is more expressive of reverence.

﴿And if you are in a state of janabah (major impurity), then purify yourselves﴾, that is: wash your bodies. ﴿And if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾. Al-Razi said: its meaning is "or has come," so that the sick person and the traveller are not obliged to perform *tayammum* without a state of *hadath*.

﴿from the Ghait (the lowered ground)﴾: a place lower than its surroundings, and it is a metaphor (*kinaya*) for relieving oneself.

﴿or you have touched women﴾: have had intercourse with them.

﴿and you find no water, then perform *tayammum* with clean earth, and wipe your faces and your hands with it. Allah does not desire to place upon you any hardship﴾: in matters of purity, so that no concession is granted to you in *tayammum*.

﴿But He desires to purify you﴾ with the dust when water is unavailable to you for purification, ﴿and to complete His favour upon you﴾, and that His favour upon you may be complete through His concessions (*rukhas*) as through His firm obligations (*'aza'im*).

﴿That perhaps you may be grateful﴾ for His favour, so that He may reward you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 7:

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾ by (granting you) Islam, ﴿and His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey."﴾ That is: He made a firm pact with you through it. It is the covenant which He took from the Muslims when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pledged them to hear and obey in ease and hardship, in what they like and what they dislike, and they accepted and said, "We hear and we obey." It is also said: it is the covenant of the night of al-'Aqabah, and the Pledge of al-Ridwan. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in breaking the covenant. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, of the secrets of hearts, of good and evil; and this is both a promise and a warning.

(p-432)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 8:

﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice﴾ bi-al-'adl (with justice) ﴿and do not let the enmity of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾

"Yajrimannakum" (لا يَجْرِمَنَّكم, "let not ... prompt you") was given the preposition of elevation (ḥarf al-isti'lā', "ʿalā") because it is made to imply a verb that takes that preposition, as if it had been said: "And let not the hatred of a people move you to abandon justice concerning them."

﴿Be just; it is nearer to righteousness﴾, i.e., justice is nearer to taqwa (God-consciousness). He first forbade them from letting hatred lead them to abandon justice, then resumed and explicitly commanded them to be just, for emphasis and reinforcement, then resumed again and mentioned to them the reason for the command to be just, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿it is nearer to righteousness﴾. If the obligation of justice toward disbelievers is of this degree of strength, then what is to be thought of its obligation toward the believers, who are its own people?! ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in what He commanded and forbade, ﴿indeed Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, a promise and a warning. For this reason, after it He mentioned the verse of promise, which is His saying, exalted is He:

The verb وَعَدَ (*wa‘ada*, "promised") is transitive to two objects (*maf‘ūlān*, "objects"). The first object is ﴿those who believe﴾, and the second is omitted. It is dispensed with by the clause which is His saying: ﴿for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. The threat (*wa‘īd*) is His saying:
​﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ — meaning: they will never depart from it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verse 11:

﴿O you who believe, remember the favor of God upon you when a people resolved to extend their hands against you﴾ It is narrated that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went to the Banu Qurayzah, and with him were the two elders, Abu Bakr and Umar, and the two in-laws (al-khatanan), asking them for the blood money (diyah, compensation for a killing) of two Muslim men whom 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri had killed by mistake, thinking they were two polytheists. They said, 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim, sit down until we feed you and lend you [the money].' They seated him in a suffah (a raised bench or platform), and they resolved to kill him. 'Amr ibn Jihash went to a huge millstone to drop it on him, but God restrained his hand. Gabriel descended and informed him of that, so the Prophet (ﷺ) left, and the verse was revealed." Here, *idh* (when) is an adverbial clause (zarf) modifying "favor."

﴿that they would stretch out﴾: that they would stretch out ﴿to you their hands﴾ with killing. It is said, "He stretched out his tongue against him" when he insulted him, and "He stretched out his hand against him" when he attacked him violently.

﴿And they stretch out to you their hands and their tongues with evil﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 2]. The meaning of stretching out the hand is extending it toward the one being attacked.

﴿So He restrained their hands from you﴾: He prevented them from being extended against you. ﴿And fear God, and upon God let the believers rely﴾: for He is the Sufficient, the Repeller, and the Preventer.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 12:

﴿And certainly Allah took the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders (nuqaba')﴾ He is the one who searches out (yunaqqibu) the conditions of the people and inquires into them. When the Children of Israel settled in Egypt, after the destruction of Pharaoh, Allah commanded them to set out for Ariha, the land of Syria, which was inhabited by the Canaanites, who were tyrannical giants. He said to them: "Indeed I have written it for you as a dwelling and a home, so go forth into it, fight those who are in it, and I will be your helper." Allah commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to take from each tribe a leader (naqib) who would stand as a guarantor over his people for their fulfilment of what they were commanded, as a pledge upon them. The leaders were chosen, the covenant was taken from the Children of Israel, and the leaders vouched for them. He set out with them, and when he drew near the land of Canaan, he sent the leaders to spy out the land. They saw enormous bodies, strength and might, so they became fearful and returned, and they reported to their people, although he (Musa) had forbidden them from informing them. So they broke the covenant, except Caleb son of Yuqanna and Joshua son of Nun, and both were among the leaders. ﴿And Allah said: "Indeed I am with you"﴾ meaning: your helper and your supporter. Here one pauses (taqif huna) before beginning the conditional clause introduced by the preparatory lam that precedes the oath, which is ﴿If you establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾, and these two were obligatory upon them, ﴿and believe in My messengers﴾ without distinguishing between any of them, ﴿and support them (wa 'azzartumuhum)﴾ and honour them, or help them by warding off their enemies from them. Al-'Azr in the language means repelling; it is said: "'azzartu fulanan", meaning: I disciplined him, i.e., you did to him what restrains him from the ugly. Thus al-Zajjaj said.

﴿And you lend Allah a goodly loan﴾ without reminding of favour; and it is said it is every good deed.

﴿Surely I will remove from you your evil deeds﴾ The lam is the answer to the oath, and this answer stands in place of the answer to both the oath and the condition together.

﴿And surely I will admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever among you disbelieves after that﴾ meaning: after that emphasised condition connected to the great promise, ﴿has indeed strayed from the right way﴾ he has erred from the path of truth. Yes, whoever disbelieved before that has also indeed strayed from the right way, but the straying after it is more evident and greater.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 13:

﴿So for their breaking their covenant﴾ "Ma" is redundant (ma' zā'ida), used to emphasize the gravity of the matter.

﴿We cursed them﴾ We drove them away and expelled them from Our mercy, or We transformed them (into apes and swine), or We imposed the jizya (poll tax) upon them.

﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾ dry, having no mercy in them and no softness. (Qasiyyah) is read by Hamza and Ali, meaning "bad," from the expression "dirham qasiyy," i.e., a debased dirham.

﴿They distort words from their places﴾ they interpret them in a way other than what was revealed. This is an explanation of the hardness of their hearts, because there is no hardness greater than fabricating lies against Allah and altering His revelation. ﴿And they have forgotten a portion﴾ and abandoned a generous share and a full measure.

﴿Of that which they were reminded﴾ of the Torah. That is, their abandonment and turning away from the Torah means neglecting a great portion. Or their hearts became hard and corrupted, so they distorted the Torah, and some of its content slipped from their memory. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "A person may forget some knowledge because of sin," and he recited this verse. It has also been said: or they abandoned their own portion of what they were commanded, namely faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) and clarifying his description.

﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾ O Muhammad, ﴿treachery from them﴾ meaning this is their habit, and their predecessors were upon it: they betrayed the messengers, and these betray you, intending to assassinate you. His saying ﴿on treachery﴾ means: upon betrayal, or upon an act characterized by betrayal, or upon a treacherous soul or a treacherous group. It is said: "rajul khā'ina" (a treacherous man), like their saying "rajul rāwiya lil-shi'r" (a man who transmits poetry), for emphasis (hyperbole).

﴿Except a few of them﴾ namely those among them who believed. ﴿So pardon them﴾ this is an encouragement to oppose them, or: pardon their believers and do not hold them accountable for what passed from them. ﴿And overlook; indeed Allah loves the good-doers﴾

14. The "min" (مِنْ) in His words ﴿And among those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant﴾, which is the covenant of belief in God, the messengers, and good deeds, is connected to "akhadhna" (We took). The meaning is: "And We took the covenant of those who say, 'We are Christians,' from them." The prepositional phrase (min alladhina) is placed before the verb, and the prepositional phrase separates the verb from the conjunction "wa" (and). The reason they are not called "min al-Nasara" (from the Christians) is that they named themselves thus, claiming to be "helpers of God" (nasr Allah). They are the ones who said to Jesus, ﴿We are God's helpers﴾. Then they disagreed after (the sects of) the Nestorians (Nasturiyya), the Jacobites (Ya'qubiyya), and the Melkites (Malkaniyya), who became helpers of Satan.

﴿But they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of, so We stirred up﴾ means "We attached and bound," from "ghara bi-l-shay'" when one clings to a thing and sticks to it. From this comes "al-ghira'" (glue), which is used for sticking things together.

﴿among them﴾ means among the differing sects of the Christians. ﴿enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is due to their divergent desires. ﴿And God will surely inform them of what they used to do﴾ means: on the Resurrection Day, with reward and punishment.

O People of the Scripture (Ahl al-Kitab)! ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ is an address to the Jews and the Christians, and "the Scripture" (al-Kitab) is used in the generic sense.

﴿There has come to you Our Messenger﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture﴾ such as the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and such as the stoning (rajm) and the like. ﴿And he pardons much﴾ of what you conceal, not making it clear. Or it means: he pardons many of you, not calling you to account for them.

﴿There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ He means the Qur'an, because it removes the darkness (zulumat) of polytheism and doubt, and because it makes clear the truth that was hidden from people; or because it is manifestly miraculous (i'jaz). Or "the light" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), because people are guided by him, just as he was named a lamp (siraj).

﴿Allah guides by it﴾, i.e., by the Qur'an, ﴿whoever follows His good pleasure﴾, and whoever among them believes, ﴿to the paths of peace﴾, the ways of safety and deliverance from the punishment of Allah. Or it means the paths of Allah. So "al-salam" means safety, or it is Allah Himself. ﴿And He brings them out of darknesses into light﴾, from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of Islam, ﴿by His permission﴾ [by His will and His enabling success], ﴿and guides them to a straight path﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 17:

﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ Its meaning is: they have definitively asserted that Allah is the Messiah and nothing else. It is said: there were among the Christians a people who said this. Or it is because their doctrine leads to it, since they believed that he creates, gives life, and causes death.

﴿Say, "Who could prevent Allah at all﴾ means: who could withhold anything from His power and His will? ﴿if He willed to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth entirely?"﴾ That is: if He willed to destroy those whom they called a god, namely the Messiah and his mother. The meaning is that the Messiah is a created servant like the rest of the servants. "And everyone on earth entirely" is conjoined to the Messiah and his mother to make clear that they are of the same kind as them, with no difference between them and others. The meaning is: how could one who was enveloped by the womb of motherhood (al-umumiyya) escape the deficiency of humanity (al-bashariyya)? And how could one upon whom the signs of createdness (al-hadathiyya) have appeared deserve the description of lordship (al-rububiyya)? And if He cut off continuance from all that He brought into existence, deficiency would not return to the self-sufficiency (al-samadiyya) of God.

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. He creates what He wills﴾ That is: He creates from a male and a female, and He creates from a female without a male, as He created Jesus, [and He creates from a male without a female, as He created Eve from Adam], and He creates without male and female, as He created Adam. Or: He creates as He wills, like the creation of birds by the hand of Jesus as a miracle for him. There is no objection to Him, for He is the Doer of whatever He wills. ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 18:

﴿And the Jews and the Christians said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones."﴾ That is: dear ones to Him, like a son to a father; or they were the followers of the two sons of Allah: ʿUzayr and the Messiah. Just as it was said of the followers of Abu Khubayb, who was ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, that they were called "al-Khubaybiyyun" (the Khubaybites). Just as the followers of Musaylima used to say: "We are the sons of Allah," and the kinsmen and attendants of a king say: "We are the sons of kings." Or it means: "We are the sons of the messengers of Allah."

﴿Say: "Why then does He punish you for your sins?"﴾ That is: if it is true that you are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones, then why are you punished for your sins, by being transformed and by the Fire, for a number of days (ayyaman maʿdudah), according to your claim? Does a father transform his son? Does a parent punish his child with the Fire? Then He said, refuting them: ﴿Rather, you are human beings among those He has created.﴾ That is: you are creatures among His creation, not His offspring.

﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾ those who repent of disbelief, by His bounty, ﴿and He punishes whom He wills﴾ those who die upon it, by His justice. ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and to Him is the final return.﴾ In this is an indication of the servitude of the Messiah, because kingship and prophethood are mutually exclusive.

(p-438)

O People of the Book, ﴿Our Messenger has certainly come to you﴾ [i.e., Muhammad (ﷺ)], ﴿making clear to you﴾. The object is omitted, meaning "the laws" (al-sharā'i'), because it is evident. Alternatively, the object is "what you used to conceal" (mā kuntum tukhfūn), and it is omitted because it was mentioned earlier. Or the object is not to be supplied, and the meaning is: he offers you clarification (yabdhulu lakumu al-bayān). In this case, the word ﴿يُبَيِّنُ﴾ (yubayyinu, "making clear") is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning "clarifying for you."

﴿عَلى فَتْرَةٍ مِنَ الرُسُلِ﴾ [after an interval (fatrah) without messengers] is connected to "جاءَكُمْ" (jā'akum, "has come to you"). That is, he came to you at a time of lull in the sending of messengers and a cutting off of revelation (waḥy). Between ʿĪsā and Muḥammad, peace be upon them both, there were six hundred years, or five hundred and sixty years.

﴿أنْ تَقُولُوا﴾ [lest you should say], out of aversion (karāhatan), ﴿أنْ تَقُولُوا﴾ [that you should say] ﴿ما جاءَنا مِن بَشِيرٍ ولا نَذِيرٍ﴾ [No bringer of good news and no warner came to us]. The fāʾ in ﴿فَقَدْ جاءَكُمْ﴾ [So indeed there has come to you] is connected to an omitted element, meaning: do not make excuses, for there has come to you ﴿بَشِيرٍ﴾ [a bringer of good news] for the believers ﴿وَنَذِيرٌ﴾ [and a warner] for the disbelievers. The meaning is a favour upon them: the Messenger was sent to them when the traces of revelation had been effaced and they were most in need of him, so that they would welcome him, regard him as the greatest blessing from Allah, and be bound by the proof, so that they could not plead tomorrow that no one had been sent to them to awaken them from their heedlessness. ﴿وَاللهُ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ [And Allah is capable of all things], so He was necessarily capable of sending Muḥammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 20:

﴿And when Musa said to his people: "O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you, when He appointed among you prophets﴾ — because no nation was sent as many prophets as the Children of Israel were sent. ﴿And made you kings﴾ — because He gave them kingship after Fir'awn (Pharaoh) had his kingdom, and after the tyrants had their kingdoms. Also, because kings were numerous among them, as prophets were numerous among them. It was also said: the malik (king) is one who has a spacious dwelling in which there is flowing water, and their dwellings were spacious, with flowing waters in them. It was also said: the king is one who has a house and servants. And also, because they had been enslaved in the hands of the Copts, and Allah rescued them, so He called their rescue "kingship." ﴿And gave you what He had not given to anyone else among the worlds﴾ — from the splitting of the sea, the drowning of the enemy, the sending down of the manna and quails, the shading of the clouds, and similar great matters; or he meant the scholars of their time.

O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you. [Al-Nasafi:] "Holy" means purified, or blessed. It is the land of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), or al-Sham (Greater Syria).

"Which Allah has prescribed for you": He has allotted it to you, or named it for you, or has written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) that it shall be your dwelling.

"And do not turn back on your heels": do not return on your tracks, fleeing in defeat out of fear of the tyrants, out of cowardice; or, do not turn back on your heels in your religion, "for you would then turn back as losers": you would return having lost the reward of this world and the Hereafter.

ﷺ

"They said, 'O Musa, indeed in it there is a people of tyrants (jabbarin). And indeed we will never enter it [by fighting] until they leave it [without fighting]. So if they leave it [without fighting], then indeed we will enter [its lands]."

Al-jabbar is on the pattern fa''al, from jabarahu 'ala al-amr, meaning ajbarahu 'alayhi (to compel him to it), and it is the haughty one who compels people to what he wishes.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 23:

﴿Said two men﴾: Kaleb (Kālib) and Yusha' (Yūshaʿ).

﴿From among those who fear﴾ Allah, and who stand in awe of Him. It is as if it were said: two men from among the God-fearing (al-muttaqūn). It is in the nominative position (maḥall al-rafʿ) as an attributive adjective (ṣifah) of "two men." Likewise, ﴿upon whom Allah had bestowed favour﴾ by fearing Him. ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾, that is, the gate of the city. ﴿For when you enter it, you will surely be victorious﴾, that is, they (the enemy) will be routed and the victory will be yours. They knew this through the informing of Musa, upon him be peace. ﴿And upon Allah rely, if you are believers﴾, since belief in Him necessitates relying upon Him, and that is cutting off attachments and abandoning flattery toward creatures.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 24:

﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed we will never enter it"﴾: this is a categorical negation of their entering it in the future, for the sake of emphasis (tawkid). ﴿Ever﴾: this links the emphasized negation to a long span of time. ﴿As long as they remain in it﴾: an explanation of "ever." ﴿So go, you and your Lord﴾: Among the scholars, some took this in its apparent (zahir) sense and said: "This is disbelief on their part." That is not so, for had they said this as a belief, and disbelieved in it, Musa would have fought them, and fighting the tyrants (al-Jabbarin) would not have been more deserving than fighting these. Rather, the correct interpretation is that it should be said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord﴾ means "your Lord helps you in your fighting." Or ﴿and your Lord﴾ means "and your master," and he is ﴿your elder brother Harun.﴾ Or the literal sense of going was not intended, but as we say, "I spoke to him, and he went to answer me," meaning the sense of intention; as if they said, "I intend to fight them." ﴿So fight, indeed we are sitting here﴾: remaining (makithun), we will not fight them for the sake of your religion. ﴿So when they disobeyed him and opposed him﴾.

﴿He said, "My Lord, I have no control except over myself and my brother"﴾ (for the support of Your religion). The word ﴿وأخِي﴾ (wa-akhī, "and my brother") is in the accusative by coordination (ʿaṭf, grammatical conjunction-linking) with "myself" (نَفْسِي), or with the subject of inna (ism inna, the noun following the particle inna), meaning: "I have no control except over myself, and indeed my brother has no control except over himself." It may also be in the nominative by coordination with the grammatical position (maḥall) of inna and its subject, or by coordination with the pronoun in "I have no control" (لا أمْلِكُ), and this is permissible because of the separation (faṣl, intervening words), meaning: "and my brother has no control except over himself." Or it is a subject (mubtada', topic of a nominal sentence) whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: "and my brother is likewise." This is a pouring out of grief (bath) and complaint to God, and a tenderness of heart by which mercy is drawn down and support is brought down. It seems that he did not trust the two men mentioned completely, so he mentioned only the infallible Prophet. Or he intended: "and whoever is united with me in my religion."

﴿So separate us from the defiantly disobedient people﴾: separate us from them and divide between us and them, by judging for us in what they deserve. This has the sense of a supplication against them. Or: distance us from one another, and deliver us from their companionship, like His saying: ﴿and save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Tahrim: 11].

Al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil (Commentary) on surah 5, verse 26:

﴿He said: "It is forbidden to them"﴾ — that is, the Holy Land — ﴿for forty years﴾ — they will not enter it. This is a prohibition of prevention (tahrim man'), not a prohibition of worship (tahrim ta'abbud), like His saying: ﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses﴾ [al-Qasas: 12]. What is meant by His saying ﴿God has prescribed for you﴾ is: on condition that you fight its people. When they refused to fight, it was said: ﴿It is forbidden to them﴾. Or the meaning is: ﴿It is forbidden to them for forty years.﴾ When the forty years had passed, what had been prescribed came about. Moses, peace be upon him, set out with those of the Children of Israel who remained, with Joshua (Yusha') at his vanguard, and he conquered it, and remained there for as long as God willed, and then he died.

"Forty" (arba'in) is the adverbial complement of the prohibition, and the pause is on "year" (sanah). Alternatively, "forty" is the adverbial complement of ﹤They wander in the land﹥, i.e., they travel in it bewildered, not finding the way, for forty years, and the pause is on "upon them" ('alayhim). They were punished with confinement because of their choice of remaining (al-mukth) in one place. So, despite the intensity of their travel, they would wake up where they had been at dusk, and be at dusk where they had woken up, within a distance of six farsakh. When he (Moses) regretted supplicating against them, it was said to him: ﹤So do not grieve over the defiant people﹥, i.e., do not sorrow over them, for they are defiant.

It has been said: Moses and Aaron were not with them in the wandering (al-tih), because it was a punishment, and Moses had asked his Lord that He separate them from them. It has also been said: they were with them, but that was a comfort (rawh) for them both and a peace, not a punishment. Aaron died during the wandering, and Moses died in it a year after him. All the chiefs (al-nuqaba') died in the wandering except Caleb (Kalib) and Joshua (Yusha').

God Most High commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to relate to those who envied him what happened because of envy, so that they would abandon it and believe, by His saying: ﴿And recite to them﴾ to the People of the Book, ﴿the account of the two sons of Adam﴾, and from his loins, Habil (Abel) and Qabil (Cain), or they were two men from the Children of Israel.

﴿with the truth﴾: an account mingled with truthfulness, in agreement with what is in the books of the earlier peoples. Or a recitation mingled with truthfulness and correctness. Or, ﴿And recite to them﴾ while you are upright and truthful.

﴿when they both offered a sacrifice﴾: this is in the accusative, governed by "the account", meaning their story and narrative at that time. Or it is an apposition to "the account", meaning: recite to them the account of that time, with the omission of a modifier (the story of) understood. ﴿a sacrifice (qurban)﴾: what one draws near to God by, of a sacrificial animal (nasikah) or a charity. It is said: he offered a charity (qarraba sadaqah) and drew near by it (taqarraba biha), because taqarraba is the intransitive form (mutawa'ah) of qarraba. The meaning: when each of them offered his sacrifice. The proof is: ﴿and it was accepted from one of them﴾, his sacrifice, and he was Habil.

﴿and it was not accepted from the other﴾, his sacrifice, and he was Qabil. It is related that God Most High revealed to Adam that he should marry each of them to the twin of the other. Qabil's twin was more beautiful, and her name was Iqlima. So his brother envied him for her, and he was enraged. Adam said to them both: "Offer a sacrifice, and whichever of you is accepted will marry her." Habil's sacrifice was accepted, in that a fire descended and consumed it. Qabil's envy and rage increased, and he threatened him with killing.

﴿He said: "I will surely kill you"﴾, that is, Qabil said to Habil. ﴿He said: "God only accepts from the righteous"﴾. Its implied meaning: He said: "Why are you killing me?" He said: "Because God accepted your sacrifice and did not accept mine!" So he said: ﴿God only accepts from the righteous﴾, and you are not righteous, so you were only brought low from your own side, by your stripping yourself of the garment of piety, not from my side.

And it is related from Amir ibn Abd Allah that he wept when death came upon him. It was said to him: "What makes you weep, when you were such-and-such?" He said: "I hear God saying: ﴿God only accepts from the righteous﴾."

"If you stretch out your hand against me to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 28:

﴿لَئِنْ بَسَطْتَ﴾ (If you stretch out) ﴿إلَيَّ يَدَكَ لِتَقْتُلَنِي ما أنا بِباسِطٍ﴾ (your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not stretch out) ﴿بِمادٍّ﴾ (my hand) — (يَدِيَ) with the reading of Madani, Abu 'Amr and Hafs (i.e., the word يَدِيَ is read with a ya' of the first person, and the variant readings are attributed to these readers).

﴿لأقْتُلَكَ إنِّي أخافُ اللهَ رَبَّ العالَمِينَ﴾ (to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds.) It is said: he (Habil) was stronger than the killer and more capable of seizing (him), but he refrained from killing his brother and submitted to him out of fear of Allah the Exalted, because repelling (the attack) was not permissible at that time. And it is said: rather, that was obligatory, for in it (fighting back) would be the destruction of his own soul and his partnership with the killer in his sin. Its meaning is only: "I shall not stretch out my hand toward you initiating (the attack), as you intend that toward me." Habil was resolved to defend himself if he intended to kill him, and he (Qabil) only killed him by treachery, while he was heedless. (إنِّي أخافُ) — the reading of the Hijazi (Ibn Kathir and Nafi' in some transmissions) and Abu 'Amr.

"Indeed, I want" — (inni) is read with the ya' of the first person (madani, i.e., the Madani reading); "that you bear" — that you take on, or that you return with;

"the sin of me" — the sin of killing me, if you kill me; "and your sin" — the sin on account of which your offering was not accepted. It is disobedience to the father, envy, and rancour. He only wanted that because of his disbelief, in rejecting the decree of Allah the Exalted, or he was a wrongdoer, and it is permissible that the recompense of the wrongdoer be what is intended: ﴿so you will be among the companions of the Fire, and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾.

Fa-tawwaat lahu nafsuhu qatla akhihi ("So his soul made the killing of his brother easy for him"): fa-wasi'athu wa-yassarat-hu, from ṭā'a lahu al-mar'ā, meaning "the pasture was spacious for him" when it expanded.

﴿Then he killed him﴾: at the slope of Ḥirāʾ, or in Basra, and the one killed was twenty years old. ﴿So he became one of the losers﴾

﴿Then God sent a raven, scratching in the earth, to show him﴾ — i.e., God, or the raven.

﴿how to conceal the shameful part (sawʾah) of his brother﴾ — the nakedness (ʿawrah) of his brother, and whatever part of his body it is not permissible to expose.

It is related that he was the first person ever killed upon the face of the earth from among the sons of Adam. When he had killed him, he left him in the open, not knowing what to do with him, and he feared for him from wild beasts, so he carried him on his back in a bag for a year until he rotted, and the wild beasts gathered around him. Then God sent two ravens, which fought, and one of them killed the other; it dug a hole for it with its beak and its feet, then threw it into the pit. At that point ﴿he said: "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this raven and conceal the shameful part of my brother?"﴾ — this is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "an akūna" (that I be). ﴿So he became one of the regretful﴾ — regretful over his killing, because of the toil he had endured in carrying him and his bewilderment about his affair. He did not feel the regret of those who repent, or the regret was a repentance specific to us, or it was regret over carrying him and not over killing him.

It is also related that when he killed him, his body turned black, though it had been white. Adam asked him about his brother, and he said: "I was not a guardian over him." Adam said: "Rather, you killed him, and that is why your body has blackened; the blacks (al-sudan) are from his offspring."

As for what is reported, that Adam elegized him with poetry, this is not authentic, because the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from poetry (al-shiʿr).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 32:**

﴿Because of that﴾: on account of that, and for that reason. "That" refers to the killing mentioned. It has been said that it is connected to the previous verse, so one stops at "that," meaning: ﴿he became one of the regretful﴾ because of carrying his body and because of killing him. It has also been said that it is a new sentence (mustaʾnaf), so one stops at "the regretful," and "min" (because of) is connected to "We prescribed," not to "the regretful." ﴿We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾: He singled them out for mention, although everyone shares in this, because the Torah was the first Book in which legal rulings appeared. ﴿That whoever kills a soul﴾: the pronoun refers to the matter (al-shan), and "whoever" (man) is conditional. ﴿Not for a soul﴾: not in retaliation for killing a soul. ﴿Or for corruption in the land﴾: this is coordinated with "soul," meaning: not for corruption in the land, which is polytheism, or highway robbery, or any corruption that requires execution.

﴿It is as if he had killed all mankind﴾: that is, in terms of the sin, according to al-Hasan (al-Basri), because the recompense of one who kills a soul is Hell, the wrath of God upon him, and a great punishment. Even if he had killed all mankind, it would not increase beyond this.

﴿And whoever gives it life﴾: and whoever rescues it from the causes of destruction, whether killing, drowning, burning, collapse, or other than these.

﴿It is as if he had given life to all mankind﴾: he made the killing of one person like the killing of all, and likewise the giving of life, as encouragement and warning. For one who intends to kill a soul, if he imagines that killing it is like killing all people, its magnitude weighs on him and it deters him. Likewise, one who intends to preserve a soul, if he imagines that its ruling is the ruling of preserving all people, he is eager to preserve it.

﴿And certainly there came to them﴾: that is, to the Children of Israel,

﴿Our messengers﴾: (rusulunā) Abu ʿAmr read it as rusulnā, with the sin (ر) pronounced with sukūn. ﴿with the clear proofs﴾: with the manifest signs.

﴿Then indeed many of them after that﴾: after what We had prescribed for them, or after the coming of the messengers with the signs.

﴿in the land are truly transgressors﴾: in killing, not caring about its enormity.

Translation of the passage:

﴿Except for those who repent before you have power over them.﴾ Then these prescribed penalties (ḥudūd) are dropped from them, but not what is the right of the servants (ḥaqq al-ʿibād), [meaning that the rights of people are not dropped]. ﴿So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ He forgives them through repentance, and has mercy on them, so He does not punish them.

"O you who believe, fear Allah" — so do not harm the servants of Allah. "And seek the means (al-wasilah) to Him" — al-wasilah is everything by which one seeks nearness; that is, one draws near through kinship, a favour, or something else. It was then borrowed (istu'īra) for that by which one seeks a means to Allah the Exalted, namely performing acts of obedience and abandoning sins. "And strive in His cause, that you may prosper."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, even if they had everything on the earth in its entirety﴾ of kinds of wealth ﴿and the like of it with it﴾ and spent it ﴿to ransom themselves thereby﴾, that is, to make it a ransom (fidyah) for their own selves. And "law" (even if) together with "ma" (what) within its scope is the predicate (khabar) of "inna" (indeed). The pronoun referring back in ﴿to ransom themselves thereby﴾ is singular, though two things have been mentioned, because he treated the pronoun as functioning like the demonstrative (ism al-ishara), as if it had been said: "to ransom themselves with that." ﴿From the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it will not be accepted from them, and for them is a painful punishment﴾. So there is no way for them to salvation by any means.
"They desire" (yuridūna): they seek, or they wish. "To come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it, and theirs is a lasting punishment" (wa-lahum ʿadhābun muqīm): constant, everlasting.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 38:

﴿And the male thief and the female thief﴾ are in the nominative by way of the inceptive (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is omitted; its estimated form is: "and" among what is recited to you "the male thief and the female thief." Or the predicate is ﴿then cut off their hands﴾, meaning their two hands, and what is intended is the right hands, as evidenced by the reading of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. The entry of the fa' (fa, the particle of consequence) is because the two of them imply the meaning of a condition (sharth), since the meaning is: "the one who stole, and the one who stole [feminine]: ﴿then cut off their hands﴾." The relative construction (al-ism al-mawsul) is treated as containing the meaning of a condition. He began with the man because theft stems from boldness, and it is more common among men; and he delayed mention of the adulterer because fornication arises from desire, and it is more abundant among women. The hand was cut off because it is the instrument of theft, while the instrument of fornication was not cut off, in order to avoid cutting off offspring (p-446). ﴿As a recompense for what they earned﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). ﴿A deterrent from God﴾ meaning a punishment from Him, and it is a substitute (badal) for "recompense." ﴿And God is Mighty﴾, dominant, not opposed in His judgment. ﴿Wise﴾ in what He decreed of cutting off the hand of the male thief and the female thief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 39:

﴿But whoever repents﴾ from the thieves ﴿after his wrongdoing﴾, that is, his theft, ﴿and makes amends﴾ by returning what was stolen, ﴿indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness﴾, that is, He will accept his repentance. ﴿Indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾, that is, He will forgive his sin and show him mercy.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 40:

﴿Do you not know﴾ O Muhammad, or O addressee, ﴿that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills﴾ (i.e., whoever dies in disbelief), ﴿and forgives whom He wills﴾ (i.e., whoever repents from disbelief), ﴿and Allah is over all things﴾ (i.e., over punishment, forgiveness, and other things).

﴿Competent﴾: capable. He placed punishment before forgiveness here because the thief (al-sariq) is mentioned before the one who repents (al-tawbah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 41:

﴿O Messenger, let not those grieve you who race to disbelief﴾. That is: do not be concerned, and do not mind the hastening of the hypocrites into disbelief, that is, in displaying it, by what appears from them of the signs of plotting against Islam and of allying with the polytheists. For I am your helper against them, and sufficient for you against their evil. It is said: "Grey hair hastened into him (asra'a fihi al-shayb)," meaning it reached him swiftly. Likewise, their hastening into disbelief is their falling into it most swiftly; whenever they find an opportunity, they do not miss it. ﴿Among those who say﴾ is an explanation of His words ﴿those who race to disbelief﴾. ﴿"We believe"﴾ is the object of "say" (qalu). ﴿With their mouths﴾ is related to "say" (qalu), that is: they say with their mouths: "We believe."

﴿But their hearts have not believed﴾: this is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿And among those who are Jews (hadu)﴾ is conjoined to ﴿among those who say﴾, that is: among the hypocrites and the Jews. ﴿Listeners to falsehood (sammaʿuna lil-kadhib)﴾ is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they are listeners, the pronoun referring to both groups; or "listeners" is the subject and its predicate is ﴿among those who are Jews﴾. On this reading, one pauses at "their hearts," and on the first reading, at "hadu."

﴿Listeners to falsehood﴾: they listen to you in order to lie about you, by distorting what they heard from you through addition, subtraction, substitution and alteration.

﴿Listeners for another people who have not come to you﴾: that is, they listen to you on behalf of another people from among the Jews, who sent them as spies, so that they might convey to them what they heard from you. ﴿They distort the words after their (proper) places﴾: that is, they remove them and turn them away from their places in which Allah placed them, so they put them in no place, after it had a place.

﴿They distort﴾ is a description of "a people," like His words ﴿who have not come to you﴾, or it is a predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they distort. The pronoun refers back to the wording "the words." ﴿They say: If you are given this﴾, meaning the distorted word removed from its places, and "they say" is like "they distort." It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "they distort."

﴿Then take it﴾: know that it is the truth, and act upon it. ﴿But if you are not given it﴾, and Muhammad has issued a ruling contrary to it, ﴿then beware﴾: beware of it and of him, for it is falsehood. It is narrated that a nobleman committed adultery with a noblewoman at Khaybar, and both were married; their punishment in the Torah is stoning. They disliked stoning them because of their nobility, so they sent a group of their men to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this, and they said: "If he orders you to flog and blacken them, accept it; and if he orders you to stone them, do not accept it." So he ordered them to be stoned, and they refused to act upon it.

﴿And whomever Allah wills to test﴾: whose misguidance He wills. This is a proof against those who say that Allah wills faith but does not will disbelief.

﴿You cannot avail him anything against Allah﴾: He cut off the hope of Muhammad (ﷺ) regarding the faith of these people. ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not will to purify﴾ from disbelief, because He knew that they had chosen disbelief; and this is also a proof for us against them. ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾: for the hypocrites, exposure; and for the Jews, humiliation.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾: that is, eternal abiding in the Fire.

﴿Listeners to falsehood﴾: it is repeated for emphasis, meaning they are listeners to falsehood. Similar to it is ﴿consumers of what is unlawful (suht)﴾, and suht is everything whose earnings are not lawful. It derives from saháta, meaning to uproot, because it is stripped of blessing (mashhut al-barakah). In a hadith it is: "Bribery in judgment." They used to take bribes for rulings and for making the unlawful lawful. Read with tathqil (the doubled-consonant form) by Makki, Basri and Ali.

﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾: It is said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had the choice, when the People of the Book brought their disputes to him, between judging between them or not judging between them. It is also said that this choice was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49]. ﴿But if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all﴾, meaning they will not be able to harm you, because Allah protects you from the people. ﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice﴾, meaning with fairness, ﴿for Allah loves those who act justly﴾, meaning those who are fair.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 43:

﴿How would they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their seeking judgment from one whom they do not believe in, nor in his Book, although the ruling is explicitly stated in their own Book, which they claim to believe in.

﴿فِيها حُكْمُ اللهِ﴾ ("in which is the judgment of Allah") is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause) of "التَوْراةِ" (the Torah). "هي" (it) is a *mubtada'* (subject), and its *khabar* (predicate) is "عِنْدَهُمْ" ("with them").

﴿ثُمَّ يَتَوَلَّوْنَ مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("then they turn away after that") is a *ʿaṭf* (conjunction) upon "يُحَكِّمُونَكَ" ("they make you judge"). That is: then, after seeking your judgment, they turn away from your ruling, which agrees with what is in their Book, and they are not pleased with it. ﴿وَما أُولَئِكَ بِالمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and those are not believers") in you, or in their Book, as they claim.

(p-٤٤٩)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 44:

﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance﴾ leading to the truth, ﴿and light﴾ clarifying what was ambiguous of the rulings. ﴿By it the prophets who submitted (aslamu)﴾ submitted (inqada) to the judgment of God in the Torah. This is a description applied to the prophets by way of praise, and its application is intended as an indirect reproach to the Jews, because they are remote from the religion of Islam (millat al-Islam), which is the religion of all the prophets.

﴿For those who became Jews (hadu)﴾ repented of disbelief. The lam (for "li-") is connected to "yahkumu" (judge).

﴿And the rabbis (rabbaniyyun) and the scholars (ahbar)﴾ are conjoined to "the prophets," meaning: the ascetics and the scholars. ﴿By what they were entrusted with (istuhfizu)﴾ they were given custody (istuwdi'u). It has been said that it may be a substitute (badal) for "bi-ha" in ﴿judges by it﴾, ﴿of the Book of God﴾, from "al-tabyin" (clarification). The pronoun in "istuhfizu" refers to the prophets, the rabbis, and the scholars all together, and the entrusting (istihfaz) is from God, meaning God charged them with its preservation. Or it refers to "the rabbis and the scholars," and the entrusting is from the prophets. ﴿And they were witnesses over it﴾ (shuhada'), guardians (ruqaba') lest it be altered. ﴿So do not fear the people﴾: this is a prohibition to the rulers against fearing other than God in their governments, and in enforcing them contrary to what they were commanded of justice, out of fear of an oppressive sultan, or fear of harm from anyone.

﴿And fear Me﴾ in opposing My command. Reading both with the ya' is easy (sahl); Abu 'Amr agreed with him in connected recitation (al-wasl).

﴿And do not trade My signs﴾ and do not exchange the signs of God and His rulings ﴿for a small price﴾, which is bribery, seeking status, and seeking the approval of people. ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has sent down﴾ while treating it with contempt (mustahinan bihi) ﴿those are the disbelievers﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: whoever does not judge by it while denying it is a disbeliever; but if he does not deny it, he is a wrongdoer (fasiq) and an oppressor (zalim). Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: it is general, applying to the Jews and others.

(p-450) ﴿And We prescribed for them therein﴾ and We made obligatory upon the Jews in the Torah that ﴿the soul [is taken] for the soul﴾, meaning the one who kills another soul without right is himself to be killed in return. ﴿And the eye [is taken] for the eye﴾, meaning an eye that is gouged out [is repaid by gouging the eye of the offender]; ﴿and the nose for the nose﴾, meaning a nose that is cut off [is repaid by cutting off the offender's nose]; ﴿and the ear for the ear﴾, meaning an ear that is cut off [is repaid by cutting off the offender's ear]; ﴿and the tooth for the tooth﴾, meaning a tooth that is pulled out [is repaid by pulling out the offender's tooth]; ﴿and for wounds, retaliation﴾. The word qisas (retaliation, equal requital) here means that the wound is subject to qisas, which is al-muqassah (the act of inflicting an equal injury). Its meaning is: wherever qisas is possible, it applies; otherwise, a just assessment (hukumah 'adl, i.e., compensation determined by a judge) is made.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they used not to kill a man in retaliation for a woman, so this verse was revealed.

His saying ﴿the soul [is taken] for the soul﴾ indicates that a Muslim is killed for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection), a man is killed for a woman, and a free person is killed for a slave.

Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah put all the coordinated items in the accusative, by coordination with what "anna" governs. 'Ali put them in the nominative, by coordination with the position (mahall) of "anna al-nafs", because the meaning is: ﴿And We prescribed upon them﴾ "the soul for the soul", treating kataba (We prescribed) as if it were qala (We said). The rest read all of them in the accusative, but read al-juruh (wounds) in the nominative.

Regarding al-udhn (ear): with the dhal pronounced with sukun (al-udhn) wherever Nafi' and the others read it, and with a damma (al-udhun) for the rest. Both are dialectal forms, like al-suht and al-suhut.

﴿So whoever forgoes it﴾ from among the rightful claimants, ﴿by it﴾, that is, by the qisas, and pardons the offender, ﴿it is an expiation (kaffarah) for him﴾. Thus, forgoing it is an expiation for the one who forgoes it, through his beneficence.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever gives charity of blood or less than it, it will be an expiation for him from the day his mother bore him."

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then they are the wrongdoers﴾, by refraining from that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 46:

﴿And We made them follow﴾ The meaning of qaffaytu al-shay' bi-al-shay' (qaffaytu, "I caused to follow") is: you placed it in its wake, as if it were placed behind it. It is said: qafāhu yaqfūhu (qafā, "he followed him"), when he followed him. ﴿in their footsteps﴾ in the footsteps of the prophets who submitted (aslamū), ﴿with ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary), confirming﴾ musaddiqan is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from ʿĪsā, ﴿that which was before him of the Torah. And We gave him the Injil (Gospel) in which was guidance and light, and confirming that which was before him of the Torah﴾. That is: ﴿and We gave him the Injil﴾ established ﴿in it, guidance and light, and confirming﴾. So the accusative of "muṣaddiqan" is by coordination (ʿaṭf) with thābitan, which was the element governed by "fīhi" and which took its place. And "hudan wa-nūr" is in the nominative by "thābitan", which took the place of "fīhi" (p-451). ﴿And guidance and admonition﴾ hudan and mawʿiẓatan are in the accusative as ḥāl, meaning: guiding and admonishing ﴿for the God-fearing﴾, because they benefit from it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 47:

﴿And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein﴾. And We said to them: "Judge by its ruling." The lam here is the lam of command (lam al-amr), and its original vowel is a kasra; it was made sukun because of the difficulty of a fatha, kasra, fatha sequence. (And let them judge) with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the mim is read by Hamzah, taking it as the lam of purpose (lam kay), meaning: "We caused them to follow [the prophets], so that they might believe, and so that they might judge." ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾, meaning those who depart from obedience.

Shaykh Abu Mansur, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is permissible to read this as referring to denial (al-juhud) in all three cases, so that the person is a disbeliever (kafir), a wrongdoer (zalim), and a defiant transgressor (fasiq), because the unqualified fasiq and the unqualified zalim are the disbeliever. It has also been said: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾ is a disbeliever in the blessing of Allah, a wrongdoer in his judgment, and a defiant transgressor in his action.

And We have sent down to you the Book (al-Kitab) in truth, i.e., the Qur'an. The definite article in it is for specific reference (li-l-'ahd). "In truth" means: by means of the truth, its establishing (of the truth), and making clear the right from the wrong. "Confirming" (musaddiqan) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Book." "For that which is before it" means: for what preceded it in revelation. It is said of what is before a thing that it is "between its hands" (bayna yadayhi), because what comes after it is behind it and after it, so what precedes it is in front of it and between its hands.

"Of the Book": what is meant by it is the category of the revealed books, because the Qur'an confirms all the books of Allah, so the definite article in it is for the category (li-l-jins). The meaning of its confirming the books is its agreement with them in tawhid (monotheism) and worship: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:25]. "Muhaymin" (guardian/overseer) over it means: and a witness, because it testifies to its soundness and preservation.

﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾, i.e., by what is in the Qur'an. ﴿And do not follow their desires, away from the truth that has come to you﴾: He forbade him to judge by what they had distorted and altered, relying on their statements. The phrase ﴿and do not follow﴾ is construed with the meaning of "and do not deviate," which is why it takes "an" (ʿan); as if it were said: "and do not deviate ﴿from the truth that has come to you﴾ by following their desires." Or the estimate is: "turning aside ﴿from what has come to you﴾."

﴿For each of you We have made a law (shir'ah) — a path (shari'ah) — and a clear way (minhaj)﴾, O people. Whoever argues from this that the law of those before us does not bind us has used it as evidence. Allah mentioned the sending down of the Torah upon Musa (peace be upon him), then the sending down of the Gospel upon 'Isa (peace be upon him), then the sending down of the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ), and He explained that it is not merely for hearing, but for judging by it. So He said regarding the first: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾; regarding the second: ﴿And let the people of the Gospel judge﴾; and regarding the third: ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed.﴾

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, a single group agreed upon one law. ﴿But﴾ He willed ﴿to test you﴾, to deal with you as one who tests, ﴿in what He has given you﴾ of the differing laws, so He imposed on each community what wisdom required. ﴿So race to good deeds﴾: hasten toward them and compete toward them before death overtakes you. By "good deeds" is meant everything Allah the Exalted has commanded. ﴿To Allah is your return﴾: this is a resumed clause, in the sense of giving the reason for racing to good deeds. ﴿All together﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive, and its governing element is the verbal noun in construct, since it is in the sense of: "to Him you will be returned."

﴿Then He will inform you about that over which you used to differ﴾: He will inform you of the recompense, which leaves no doubt, distinguishing between your one who is right and your one who is wrong, and between your one who acts and your one who neglects action.

"And that you judge" is coordinated with "with the truth," meaning: "We sent down to you the Book with the truth," and [We sent it down] that you judge between them by what God has sent down, and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they divert you (from) some of what God has sent down to you. "Lest they divert you" means: lest they turn you away. It is an object of purpose, meaning: for fear that they might divert you. He warned him—though he is a trustworthy messenger—in order to cut off the hopes of the people.

﴿If they turn away﴾ from judging by what God has sent down to you, and desire other than it, ﴿then know that God only desires to afflict them for some of their sins﴾, meaning: for the sin of turning away from God's judgment and desiring its opposite. He put ﴿for some of their sins﴾ in place of that. This vagueness is to magnify the turning away, and in it is a magnification of sins, for some of them are destructive, so how about all of them? ﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning: they are going out of obedience to God.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 50:

﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Time of Ignorance (al-jahiliyyah)?﴾ "yabghun" means they seek. With the ta' (﴿tabghun﴾) it is read by Ibn Amir (Shami), addressing the Banu al-Nadir regarding their preference for themselves over the Banu Qurayzah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to them: "The slain are equal," but the Banu al-Nadir said: "We do not accept that," and so this was revealed. Tawus was asked about a man who favors some of his children over others, and he recited this verse. The verb governing ﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Time of Ignorance﴾ is "yabghun." ﴿And who is better﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and its predicate, and it is an interrogative with the meaning of negation, i.e., no one is better ﴿in judgment than Allah﴾, where "judgment" (hukman) is a specification (tamyiz).

﴿for a people who are certain﴾: the lam is for explanation (lam al-bayan), like the lam in ﴿Come, I am at your disposal﴾ [Yusuf: 23]. That is: this address and this interrogation are for ﴿a people who are certain﴾, for they are the ones who come to recognize that there is no one more just than Allah, and no one better in judgment than Him. Abu 'Ali said: the meaning of "li-qawmin" is "'inda qawmin" (with a people), because the lam and "'inda" are close in meaning.

And it was revealed as a prohibition against allying with the enemies of the religion: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as awliya' (allies/protectors)﴾. That is: do not take them as allies whom you support, whom you seek support from, whom you treat as brothers, and whom you associate with in the manner of believers. Then he gave the reason for the prohibition with His words: ﴿They are allies of one another﴾, and all of them are enemies of the believers. In this there is evidence that all disbelief is one religion (millah wahidah). ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾, i.e., he is among their number, and his ruling is their ruling. This is a severe warning from Allah and an emphasis on the obligation of keeping away from those who differ in religion. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, i.e., He does not guide those who wronged themselves by allying with the disbelievers.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 52:**

﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, meaning hypocrisy, ﴿hastening toward them﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or a second object, given the possibility that "fa-tarā" (so you see) is from seeing with the eye or from seeing with the heart.

﴿Concerning them﴾, in (p-454) their assisting against the Muslims and their allegiance [to the disbelievers], ﴿saying﴾, that is, to themselves, as indicated by His saying: ﴿for what they concealed﴾, ﴿"We fear that a misfortune may befall us"﴾, that is, an event that turns against the present state in which they are. ﴿Then perhaps Allah will bring a conquest﴾ for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over his enemies, and the manifestation of the Muslims, ﴿or a command from Him﴾, that is, the Prophet (ﷺ) will be commanded to expose the concealment of the hypocrites and to kill them. ﴿Then they will become﴾, that is, the hypocrites, ﴿regretful for what they concealed within themselves﴾ of hypocrisy. ﴿Regretful﴾ is the predicate of ﴿fa-yuṣbiḥū﴾ (then they will become).

﴿And those who believe will say﴾, meaning some of them will say to one another at that time. "Wa-yaqūlu" (and [he] will say) is read by the Basran reader as coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "an yaʾtiya" (that he may bring). The Syrian and Hijazi readers read "yaqūlu" without the waw, as an answer to someone who asks: "So what will the believers say then?" And it is said: "Those who believe will say..."

﴿Are these the ones who swore by God with the utmost of their oaths that they were with you?﴾ meaning: they swore to you with the strongest oaths that they are your allies and supporters against the disbelievers. "Jahda aymānihim" (the utmost of their oaths) is an infinitive in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: striving to confirm their oaths. ﴿Their deeds have become void﴾, meaning their deeds were lost, those which they performed for show (riyāʾ, showing off) and reputation (sumʿah, seeking a name), not out of faith and conviction.
