This statement of God, Mighty and Majestic, is a testimony against them that their deeds are void, and an expression of wonder at the wretchedness of their state. ﴿So they became losers﴾, in this world and in the hereafter, through the loss of help and the endurance of punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 54:

﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾ means: whoever of you returns from the religion of Islam to what he was upon of disbelief. (يَرْتَدِدْ) [yartadid]: read by Madani and Shami (the readers of Medina and Syria).

﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him﴾: He is pleased with their deeds, praises them for them, and they obey Him and prefer His pleasure. In this is evidence of the prophethood of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, since he informed them of what had not yet happened, and it happened; and evidence for the caliphate of al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), since he fought the apostates; and regarding the soundness of his caliphate and that of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. «The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about them, so he struck the shoulder of Salman and said: "This one and his people. If faith were suspended at al-Thurayya, men from the sons of Persia would attain it."» The returning pronoun of the response to the noun that includes the meaning of the condition is omitted; its meaning is: ﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people﴾ in their place ﴿humble﴾, the plural of dhalil (humble). As for dhalul, its plural is dhulul. Whoever claims that it derives from dhull, which is the opposite of difficulty, has erred, because dhalul is not pluralized as adhillah. Al-Jawhari said: "al-dhull is the opposite of honor, and a man who is dhalil is clearly humble; a people are adhilla' and adhillah. And al-dhill, with a kasra, is gentleness, which is the opposite of difficulty; one says: a dabba dhalul (a tame animal), and dawabb dhulul."

﴿toward the believers﴾: it does not say "to (li) the believers," because humility (dhull) includes the sense of tenderness and compassion, as if it were said: compassionate toward them, in a manner of humbleness and modesty.

﴿mighty toward the disbelievers﴾: harsh toward them. Al-azazz is hard ground, so they are with the believers like a child to his father and a slave to his master, and with the disbelievers like a beast of prey upon its prey.

﴿who strive in the way of Allah﴾: they fight the disbelievers. This is a description of a people, like: whom He loves, and mighty, and humble.

﴿and do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾: the waw may be for the state (hal), meaning: they strive while their state in striving is contrary to the state of the hypocrites, for the hypocrites used to be allies of the Jews; when they went out with the army of the believers, they feared their Jewish allies, so they would not do anything which they knew would bring them blame from that quarter. As for the believers, their striving for Allah is without fear of any blamer's blame. The waw may also be for coordination (ʿatf), meaning: striving in the way of Allah is among their attributes, and they are firm in their religion when they undertake any matter of religion; the blame of a blamer does not turn them back. The lawma (blame) is a single instance of blame, and in it and in its indefiniteness there are two intensifications, as if it were said: they do not fear anything at all of a single blame from any of the blamers. ﴿That﴾ refers to what He has described the people with: love, humility, might, striving, and the absence of fear of blame. ﴿That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, abundant in bounties, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of whoever is worthy of it.

Following the prohibition against taking as allies those whose enmity is obligatory to oppose, he mentioned those whose alliance is obligatory by His saying: ﴿Your only ally is God, and His Messenger, and those who believe﴾. The word "innama" (only, exclusively) indicates that alliance is restricted to them. The word "wali" (ally) is not made plural, even though the referent is a group, as an alert that guardianship belongs primarily to God and is secondary for anyone else. Had it been said, "Your allies are only God, and His Messenger, and those who believe," there would be no principal and secondary in the statement. The position (i'rab) of ﴿those who establish the prayer﴾ is nominative, either as a substitute (badal) for "those who believe," or as the predicate of "they are those who," or accusative by way of praise (nasb 'ala al-madh).

﴿And they give zakat﴾, and the waw in ﴿while they are bowing﴾ is the waw of circumstance (wawu al-hal), meaning: they give it while in the state of bowing in prayer. It is said that it was revealed concerning 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, when a beggar asked him while he was bowing in his prayer, so he threw him his ring, as though it were loose on his little finger, and he did not exert himself to remove it with much movement that would invalidate his prayer. It came in the plural form, although the cause was one person, to encourage people to act like him so that they might obtain a similar reward. The verse indicates the permissibility of giving charity during prayer, and that a small action does not invalidate the prayer.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 56:

﴿Whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe as allies﴾ — let him take them as allies (waliyyan), or let him be an ally (waliyyan): ﴿then indeed the party of Allah, they are the victorious﴾. This is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun (iqamat al-zahir maqam al-damir, i.e., the explicit noun standing where a pronoun would normally be used), meaning: indeed they are the victorious. Or the intended meaning of "the party of Allah" is the Messenger and the believers, meaning: whoever takes them as allies has taken the party of Allah and sought support from one who cannot be overcome. The origin of hizb (party, group) is a people who gather for a matter concerning their group (hizbuhum), i.e., that which befalls them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 57:

It is related that Rifa'ah ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Harith had professed Islam, then became hypocrites (munafiqun), and some men among the Muslims were friendly with them. So there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as mockery and play﴾. It means: their taking your religion as mockery and play does not warrant that it be met with your taking them as allies; rather, it is met with enmity (al-baghda') and renunciation (al-munabadha). ﴿From among those who were given the Book﴾: "min" here is for explanation (li-l-bayan). ﴿from before you, and the disbelievers﴾, i.e., the polytheists (al-mushrikun). It is a conjunction (ataf) upon "alladhina" in the accusative position. And "al-kuffar" (with the genitive) is read by Basri and Ali as a conjunction upon the genitive "alladhina", meaning: from among those who were given the Book before you, and from among the disbelievers. ﴿as allies. And fear Allah﴾ regarding befriending the disbelievers, ﴿if you are truly believers﴾, because true faith (iman haqqan) rejects befriending the enemies of the religion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 58:

﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it as a mockery and a game.﴾ That is: they take the prayer (ṣalāh), or the calling (munādāh), as a mockery and a game.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ Because their play and mockery are among the actions of fools and ignorant people, so it is as though they have no intellect. And in this there is a proof that the adhān (call to prayer) is established by the prescription of the Book, not by dream alone.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 59:

﴿Say, "O People of the Book, do you blame us for nothing except that we believed in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before [us]?"﴾ Meaning: Do you find fault with us and object to us for nothing but believing in Allah and in all the revealed Books?! ﴿And that most of you are defiantly disobedient.﴾ This is conjoined to the genitive (majrur) noun, i.e., "You blame us for nothing except believing in Allah, and what has been revealed, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient." The meaning: Do you hold enmity against us because we hold to the Oneness of Allah and the truthfulness of His Prophets, and because of your own defiant disobedience in opposing us in that?! It is also permissible for the waw (و) to mean "with" (مع), i.e., "And you blame us for nothing except believing in Allah, along with the fact that most of you are defiantly disobedient."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 60:

﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from Allah?﴾ That is, as reward (thawab). It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Although al-Mathuba (reward) is specifically used for good, it has been placed in the position of punishment, as in His saying: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21]. The Jews used to claim that the Muslims deserved punishment, so it was said to them: ﴿Whom Allah has cursed﴾, who is in reality worse in punishment than the people of Islam in your assumption. "That" (dhalika) refers to what was mentioned earlier, i.e., (p-458) the faith, meaning: something worse, in reward, than what you resented in our faith, that is, in recompense. A genitive noun (mudaf) must be omitted before it, or before "min"; its estimate is: worse than the people of that, or the religion of those whom Allah has cursed.

﴿And He became angry with them and made of them apes﴾: meaning the people of the Sabbath. ﴿And swine﴾: that is, the disbelievers among the people of the table of 'Isa, peace be upon him. Or both transformations were of the people of the Sabbath: their youths were transformed into apes and their elders into swine. ﴿And who worshipped the Taghut﴾: that is, the calf, or Satan, because their worship of the calf was by Satan's adornment. It is a conjunction with the relative clause of "man" (who), as if it were said: "and who worshipped the Taghut." Hamzah read ﴿wa 'abida al-taghut﴾ (وَعَبِدَ الطاغُوتِ), making it a noun established for intensification, like the phrases "a man who is hadhir (very cautious)" and "fatin (very shrewd)," for one who is extreme in caution and shrewdness. It is conjoined to "apes" and "swine," meaning: Allah made of them those who worshipped the Taghut. ﴿Those﴾: the transformed, the cursed.

﴿Worse in place﴾: wickedness has been attributed to the place, while it actually belongs to its people, as an intensification.

﴿And further astray from the right way﴾: from the intended path that leads to Paradise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 61:

It was revealed concerning some of the Jews who used to enter upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and show him belief out of hypocrisy: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe," while they had entered with disbelief and they had gone out with it.﴾ The bāʾ (bi-) here is for ḥāl (circumstance), meaning: they entered as disbelievers and they went out as disbelievers. Its estimated sense is: "joined with disbelief" (multtabisīn bi-l-kufr). Likewise "qad dakhalū" (they had entered).

﴿wa-hum qad kharajū﴾: and therefore "qad" was used here to bring the past closer within the circumstance (taqrīban lil-māḍī min al-ḥāl). It is connected to "qālū āmannā" (they said, "We believe"), meaning: they said that while this was their state. ﴿And Allah knows best what they were concealing﴾ of hypocrisy.

ﷻ "And you see many of them" — of the Jews — "hastening into sin" — lying — "and transgression" — injustice. Or: sin is that which is specific to them, and transgression is that which goes beyond them to others. And "hastening (musara'ah) into a thing" means beginning it quickly. "And their devouring of what is forbidden (al-suht)" — the unlawful — "Evil indeed is what they used to do." Evil indeed is the thing they did.

"Why do not" (lawla): "Why do they not" in the sense of rebuke and urging, i.e. "would that" in the sense of reproach.

Actually, following the instructions: translate faithfully.

**Lawlā** (لَوْلا) — "why not" — meaning *halla* (هَلّا), and it is an expression of urging (taḥḍīḍ).

﴿Why do not the rabbis and the scholars forbid them from their uttering of sin and their consuming of unlawful gain? Evil indeed is what they used to do.﴾

This is a censure of the scholars, while the first (verse) is for the common people. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "It is the most severe verse in the Qur'an, for it makes one who abandons forbidding evil equal to one who commits evil in terms of the threat (of punishment)."

﴿The Jews say, "Allah's hand is chained up." Their own hands are chained up, and they are cursed for what they said. Rather, both His hands are outstretched.﴾ It is related that when the Jews, may Allah curse them, denied Muhammad (ﷺ), Allah withdrew the abundance He had bestowed upon them, and they had been among the wealthiest of people. At that point Fanhas said, "Allah's hand is chained up," and the others approved of his statement and shared in it. Chaining the hand (*ghull al-yad*) and extending it (*bast*) are figurative expressions (*majaz*) for stinginess and generosity. From this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Do not keep your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isra' 29]. The speaker does not intend by it an affirmation of a hand, nor of a chain, nor of an extension. It is even used of a king who gives and withholds by gesture without using his hand. If a one-armed man (cut off at the shoulder) gave a lavish gift, people would say, "How open-handed he is with his giving!" It is also used where a hand cannot literally apply, as in the saying, "Fear (*ba's*) spread its two palms over my chest," where Fear, which is one of the abstract meanings, is given two palms. Whoever has not studied the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-bayan*) will be bewildered in interpreting verses like this one.

As for His words ﴿their hands are chained up﴾, this is an invocation against them with stinginess, which is why they became the most miserly of Allah's creatures. Alternatively, it means that their hands will be chained in Hell, so it is as if they were already chained. The word *yad* is made dual (*thunniyat*) in ﴿but His two hands are outstretched﴾, while it is singular (*mufradah*) in their saying "Allah's hand is chained up," so that the rejection of their statement and its denial would be more emphatic, and more indicative of affirming the utmost generosity for Him and negating stinginess from Him. The utmost that a generous person can give is to give with his two hands. ﴿He spends as He wills﴾ is an emphasis on the attribute of generosity, and an indication that He spends only in accordance with wisdom. ﴿And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them﴾, that is, of the Jews, ﴿in defiance and disbelief﴾. Meaning: at the descent of the Qur'an they increase, out of their envy, in persistence in denial and in disbelief in the signs of Allah. This is the attribution of the act to its cause, as He said: ﴿so it added to them uncleanness upon their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawbah 125]. ﴿And We have placed among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾. Thus their words are always divergent and their hearts scattered, and no agreement or mutual support ever arises among them.

﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it.﴾ Every time they intended to fight anyone, they were overcome and subdued; no victory from Allah ever came to them over anyone at all. Islam came to them while they were under the rule of the Magians. It is also said: whenever they fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he was given victory over them. Qatadah said: You will not encounter a Jew in any land without finding him among the most humiliated of people. ﴿And they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾, that is, they exert effort to repel Islam and to erase the mention of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, from their books. ﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 65:

﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed﴾ in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in what he brought, along with what We have enumerated of their misdeeds, ﴿and had feared Allah﴾ — that is, they combined their belief with piety (taqwa) — ﴿We would have removed from them their misdeeds﴾ and would not have held them accountable for them, ﴿and We would have admitted them into Gardens of Bliss﴾ along with the Muslims.

And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel, meaning: upheld their rulings and their limits, and what they contain of the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿and what was sent down to them from their Lord﴾, meaning the rest of the Books of Allah, because they are obligated to believe in all of them, so it is as if they were sent down to them. It was also said that it refers to the Qur'an. ﴿They would have eaten from above them﴾, meaning the fruits from above their heads, ﴿and from beneath their feet﴾, meaning the crops. This is an expression of abundance, like the saying of people: "So-and-so is in blessing from his horn to his foot." The verse indicates that acting in obedience to Allah the Exalted is a cause of abundant provision, and it is like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 66] and ﴿And whoever is mindful of Allah, He will make for him a way out, and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2-3], and ﴿So I said: "Ask forgiveness of your Lord, indeed He is ever Forgiving"﴾, and the verses that follow [Nuh: 10 and what comes after it], and ﴿And that if they remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]. ﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾, a group whose condition is that of the nations in opposing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: they are the believing group, namely Abdullah ibn Salam (al-Salam) and his companions, and forty-eight of the Christians. ﴿And many of them, evil is what they do﴾. It carries the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "And many of them, how evil their deeds are!" It was also said: they are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and others.

﴿O Messenger, deliver what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ all of what has been sent down to you. Whatever has been sent down to you, deliver it without being concerned about anyone in conveying it, and without fearing that some harm will befall you. ﴿And if you do not﴾ means, if you do not convey all of it as I have commanded you. ﴿Then you have not conveyed His message﴾ (رِسالاتِهِ, "His messages"), a reading of Madani, Shami, and Abu Bakr. That is, you have then not conveyed what you were charged with of delivering the Message, and you have not delivered any part of it at all. This is because no part of it is more deserving of delivery than another. So if you do not deliver some of it, it is as if you have neglected delivering all of it. Likewise, whoever does not believe in some of it is like one who does not believe in all of it, because it is all under one ruling, since it falls under one address. A single thing cannot be both conveyed and not conveyed, or believed in and not believed in.

The heretics (al-Mulhida), may God curse them, said: "This statement is pointless. It is like your saying to your servant, 'Eat this food; if you do not eat it, then you have not eaten it.'" We reply: This is a command to convey the Message in the future. That is, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord in the future. ﴿If you do not﴾, that is, if you do not convey the Message in the future, then it is as if you have not conveyed the Message at all. Or it means: convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord now, and do not wait for an abundance of strength and equipment. If you do not convey it, you are like one who has not conveyed at all. Or it means: convey it without fearing anyone. If you do not convey it in this manner, it is as if you have not conveyed the Message at all.

Then He said, encouraging him to convey it: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾, that is, He will guard you from them so that they cannot kill you. Thus they were unable to do so, even though on the day of Uhud his face was wounded and his front tooth (rubā'iyyah) was broken, or [this verse] was revealed after what happened to him had happened. (p-٤٦٢) "The people" here means the disbelievers, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not guide the disbelieving people﴾, meaning He will not enable them to carry out what they wish to inflict upon you of destruction.

"Say, O People of the Book, you have no standing (lit. "you are not upon anything") — no religion that is considered valid — until it is called 'something' only in the sense of its falsehood — until you establish the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been sent down to you from your Lord." That is, the Qur'an. "And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief." The attribution of the increase in disbelief and transgression to the Qur'an is by way of causation (tasbib). "So do not grieve over the disbelieving people." Do not feel sorrow over them, for the harm of that returns to them, not to you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 69:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ (with their tongues), and they are the hypocrites. This is indicated by His words: ﴿Let not those grieve you who race to disbelief from among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths, but their hearts have not believed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]. ﴿And those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians﴾. Sibawayh and all the Basran grammarians said: al-Sabi'un is in the nominative by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, and the intention behind it is deferral from what is within the scope of "inna" (indeed), its subject and its predicate, as if it were said: Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Christians, ﴿whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾, and the Sabeans likewise, meaning: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, there is no fear for them. So he placed it first and omitted the predicate, as in his saying:

*Whoever has his dwelling in Medina at dusk* ∗∗∗ *then I and Qayyar there are indeed strangers.*

That is: then I am indeed a stranger, and Qayyar likewise. The lam indicates that it is the predicate of "inna." It is not in the nominative by coordination with the grammatical position (mahall) of "inna" and its subject, because that is not valid before the predicate is completed (p. 463). You do not say: "Indeed Zayd and 'Amr are departing," rather what is permissible is: "Indeed Zayd is departing, and 'Amr." Al-Sabi'un together with its omitted predicate forms a sentence coordinated upon the sentence of his saying, "Indeed, those who believe," to its end. It has no grammatical position (mahall), just as the sentence it is coordinated upon has none. The benefit of the fronting is to alert that the Sabeans, who are the most evident of these enumerated groups in misguidance and the most extreme in error, will be accepted from them if faith is sound from them; so what is to be thought of others?! The position of "man amana" is nominative as an inchoative, and its predicate is ﴿then there is no fear for them﴾, and the fa' (then) is because the subject contains the meaning of a condition. Then the sentence, as it is, is the predicate of "inna," and the returning pronoun to the subject of "inna" is omitted, its estimated form being: whoever of them believes.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 70:

﴿Indeed We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ concerning monotheism (tawhid), ﴿and We sent to them messengers﴾ so that they would make them aware of what they should do and what they should leave undone in their religion. ﴿Every time there came to them a messenger﴾ is a conditional clause (jumlah shartiyyah) that stands as a descriptive qualifier (sifah) for "rusulan" (messengers), and its returning pronoun (al-raji‘) is omitted, meaning: a messenger from among them. ﴿with what their souls did not desire﴾ meaning, with what opposes their desires and runs counter to their appetites, from the hardships of the obligations and the practice of the laws (shara'i‘). The answer (jawab) of the conditional is omitted, and it is indicated by ﴿a party they called liars and a party they kill﴾, as if it were said: every time a messenger from among them came to them, they opposed him. His statement ﴿a party they called liars﴾ is a resumptive answer (jawab mustani'af) for a questioner, as if he were saying: how did they treat their messengers? He used the present tense "yaqtulun" (they kill) to narrate a past situation vividly, to express the horror of the killing and to draw attention to the fact that killing was among their habits. "Fariqan" (a party) is in the accusative, and "fariqan" (the second) is also in the accusative, as the object of "kadhdhabu" (they called liars) and "yaqtulun" (they kill). It has been said: the denial is shared between the Jews and the Christians, while the killing is specific to the Jews, for they killed Zakariyya and Yahya.

(ألّا تَكُونُ) Ḥamzah, ʿAlī, and Abū ʿAmr read *ألّا تَكُونُ*, taking *"أنْ"* as *mukhaffafah* (the lightened form, from *thaqīlah*, the heavy form of *inna*). Its original form was *أنَّهُ لا تَكُونُ*. The *"أنْ"* was lightened and the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*) was omitted. Because their assumption was firmly fixed in their hearts, it was treated as knowledge (*ʿilm*). For this reason the verb of assumption (*fiʿl al-ḥusbān*) governs *"أنِ"*, which here indicates certainty (*lil-taḥqīq*). ﴿فِتْنَةٌ﴾ means affliction and punishment. That is, the Children of Israel assumed that no punishment from God would befall them for killing the prophets and denying the messengers. The *"أنْ"* clause, with its predicate and subject, stands in place of the two objects of *ḥasiba* (*saddα maqāma mafʿūlay ḥasiba*). ﴿فَعَمُوا وصَمُّوا﴾: they did not act upon what they saw or what they heard, or they were blind to right guidance and deaf to admonition. ﴿ثُمَّ تابَ اللهُ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾: God granted them repentance. ﴿ثُمَّ عَمُوا وصَمُّوا كَثِيرٌ مِنهُمْ﴾: *كَثِيرٌ* is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun, that is, the *wāw* of *عَمُوا وصَمُّوا*, and it is a *badal al-baʿḍ min al-kull* (substitution of a part for the whole). Alternatively, it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are, many of them..." ﴿واللهُ بَصِيرٌ بِما يَعْمَلُونَ﴾: God is All-Seeing of what they do, and so He will recompense them according to their deeds.

(p-٤٦٤)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 72:

﴿Indeed, they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) did not distinguish himself from them in the fact that he is a servant who is nurtured (by his Lord), so that it would be a proof against the Christians. ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah﴾ in His worship, worshipping other than Allah, ﴿Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾, which is the abode of the monotheists; that is, He has forbidden him to enter it and prevented him from it, ﴿and his refuge is the Fire﴾; that is, his final return is to it.

﴿And for the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the disbelievers, ﴿there are no helpers﴾. And this is from the words of Allah, or from the words of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verse 73:

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say: Indeed Allah is the third of three.﴾ That is: the third of three gods. The difficulty is that He, exalted is He, said in the first verse: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say: Indeed Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17], and said in the second: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say: Indeed Allah is the third of three.﴾ The answer is that some of the Christians used to say: the Messiah himself was Allah, because Allah may manifest Himself (*yatajalla*) at certain times in a person, so at that time He manifested Himself in the person of Jesus. For this reason, acts appeared from the person of Jesus that none is able to perform except Allah. And some of them went to [the belief in] three gods: Allah, Mary, and the Messiah, and that he was the son of Allah by Mary. The *min* (from) in His saying ﴿And there is no god except one God﴾ is for *al-istighraq* (comprehensive exclusion, i.e., covering every case), meaning: there is no god whatsoever in existence except a god described by oneness, having no second, and He is Allah alone, having no partner. In His saying ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, a painful punishment will touch those of them who disbelieved﴾ the *min* (of them) is for *al-bayan* (explanation), like the one in ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. He did not say "will touch them," because placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun carries a repetition of the testimony against them of disbelief. Or it is for *al-tab'id* (partition), meaning: will touch those among them who remained upon disbelief, because many of them repented from Christianity. ﴿A painful punishment﴾: a type of punishment of severe pain.

﴿Will they not then repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾ (Will they not repent, after this repeated testimony against them of disbelief and this severe warning, from what they are upon? And in it is an expression of wonder at their persistence) ﴿And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ — He forgives these people if they repent, and others too.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 75:

﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger﴾ In it is the negation of divinity from him. ﴿Messengers had passed away before him﴾ is a description of the messenger, meaning: he is nothing but a messenger of the same kind as the messengers who passed away before him. His healing of the blind and the leper, and his raising of the dead, did not come from himself, because he is not a god. Rather, God healed the blind and the leper and brought the dead to life through his hand, just as He brought the staff to life and made it a moving serpent through the hand of Moses. And He created him without a male, as He created Adam without a male or female. ﴿And his mother was a truthful woman﴾ meaning: his mother too was nothing but like some of the women who affirmed the prophets and believed in them. The title "truthful" (siddiqah) was applied to them, based on the words of God, Exalted: ﴿And she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. Then He distanced both of them from what was attributed to them by saying: ﴿They both used to eat food﴾, because whoever needs to nourish himself with food, and what follows from it of digestion and elimination, is nothing but a composite body made of flesh, bone, veins, nerves, and other things, which indicates that he is created and composed like other bodies. ﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them﴾, meaning: the evident proofs that demonstrate the falsehood of their claim. ﴿Then look how they are turned away﴾, meaning: how they are diverted from listening to the truth and reflecting upon it after this clarification. This is an expression of wonder from God, Exalted, at their neglect of the distinction between the Lord and the one who is lord.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 76:

﴿Say: Do you worship, besides Allah, that which possesses for you neither harm nor benefit?﴾ That is ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), meaning: something that is not able to harm you with the like of what Allah harms you with, such as trials and calamities in your persons and your wealth, nor to benefit you with the like of what Allah benefits you with, such as soundness of bodies, abundance, and fertility. This is because everything that humans are able to do of harm and benefit is by His creating (takhlīq), exalted is He. So it is as though he possesses none of it at all. And this is a decisive proof that his status is incompatible with lordship (rubūbiyyah), since He made him unable to bring harm or benefit, whereas the attribute of the Lord is that He is capable of everything, and nothing that is within the scope of power falls outside His power. ﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ this is connected to: "Do you worship," meaning: Do you associate partners with Allah and not fear Him, while He is the One who hears what you say and knows what you believe.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 77:

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the limits in your religion, going beyond the truth."﴾ Al-ghuluww (exceeding the limit): going beyond the bounds. The exaggeration (ghuluww) of the Christians is raising him (Jesus) above his station by ascribing to him the attributes of divinity, and the exaggeration of the Jews is lowering him from the rank of prophethood. ﴿Ghayr al-haqq (going beyond the truth)﴾ is an attribute of a omitted verbal noun (masdar), i.e., exaggeration that is not the truth, meaning: false exaggeration. ﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before, and who led many astray, and strayed from the right path.﴾ That is: your forebears and your leaders (a'immatikum) who were upon misguidance before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿And who led many astray﴾ among those who followed them. ﴿And strayed from the right path﴾ when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, when they denied him, envied him, and rebelled against him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 78:

﴿Those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved were cursed upon the tongue of David and of Jesus, son of Mary.﴾ It is said: When the people of Ayla (Eilat) transgressed concerning the Sabbath, David said: "O Allah, curse them, and make them a sign," and so they were transformed into apes. And when the companions of Jesus disbelieved after the Table (al-Ma'idah), Jesus said: "O Allah, punish whoever disbelieved after eating from the Table with a punishment You have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds, and curse them as You cursed the companions of the Sabbath," and so they became swine. They were five thousand men. ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾ That cursing was on account of their disobedience and their transgression.

Then he explained the disobedience and transgression with His words: ﴿They did not forbid one another﴾ from evil ﴿which they committed﴾ — they did not forbid one another from a repugnant act they committed. The description of the evil as "which they committed" — and forbidding does not occur after the act — means that they did not restrain one another from repeating an evil they had committed, or from the like of an evil they had committed, or from an evil they intended to commit. Or the meaning is: they did not desist from an evil they had committed, but persisted in it. It is said: "tanahā 'an al-amr" and "intahā 'anhu," meaning: he refrained from it and abandoned it. Then He expressed wonder at the evil of their deeds, emphasizing this with an oath in His words: ﴿Evil indeed is what they used to do.﴾ In this is evidence that abandoning the forbidding of evil is among the grave matters. So alas for the Muslims in their turning away from it!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 80:

﴿You see many of them taking as allies those who disbelieve.﴾ They are the hypocrites among the People of the Book, who used to take the polytheists (al-mushrikun) as allies and be friendly with them. ﴿Evil is what their souls have sent ahead for them, [for] that Allah has become angry with them.﴾ The evil thing their souls sent ahead for themselves is the anger of Allah upon them, i.e., that which necessitates the anger of Allah. ﴿And in the punishment they will abide forever.﴾ I.e., in Jahannam (Hell).

(Al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on Surah 5, verse 81)

﴿And if they had believed in Allah﴾ with sincere faith, without hypocrisy, ﴿and the Prophet﴾ — that is, Muhammad (ﷺ) — ﴿and what was revealed to him﴾ — meaning the Qur'an — ﴿they would not have taken them as allies﴾. They would not have taken the polytheists as allies; that is, allying with the polytheists indicates their hypocrisy. ﴿But many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ — persisting in their disbelief and hypocrisy. Or its meaning is: if these Jews had believed in Allah and in Moses and what was revealed to him — meaning the Torah — they would not have taken the polytheists as allies, just as the Muslims did not ally with them. ﴿But many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ — departing from their religion, so they have no religion at all.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 82:

﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews﴾. "The Jews" is the second object of "tajidanna" (you will find), and "ʿadāwatan" (in enmity) is a tamyīz (specifying accusative). ﴿And those who associated partners [with God]﴾ is conjoined to them (the Jews). ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward those who believe to be those who say, "Indeed, we are Christians."﴾ The lam (in "lilladhīna," "toward those who") is related to both "ʿadāwatan" and "mawaddatan" (affection).

He described the Jews by the severity of their disposition, and the Christians by the gentleness of their temperament. Most of the Jews are companions of the polytheists in their intense enmity toward the believers, and He drew attention to their precedence in it by placing them before the polytheists.

﴿That is because among them are qissisin (priests) and ruhban (monks)﴾, that is: scholars and worshippers.

﴿And that they are not arrogant﴾: He gave as the reason for the ease of approach of the Christians and the nearness of their affection toward the believers that among them are priests and monks, and that in them there is humility and lowliness, whereas the Jews are contrary to that.

In this is evidence that knowledge is the most beneficial thing and the most guiding to good, even if it is the knowledge of priests, and likewise the knowledge of the Hereafter even if it is found in a monk, and freedom from arrogance even if it is found in a Christian.

(p-469)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 83:

﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized﴾. He described them with tenderness of heart, and that they weep when they hear the Qur'an, as is related from al-Najashi (the Negus), that he said to Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, when the emigrants to Abyssinia and the polytheists had gathered in his assembly while they were reciting it to them: "Is there mention of Maryam (Mary) in your Book?" Ja'far said: "There is a surah named after Maryam." So he recited it up to His saying: ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary﴾ [Maryam: 34], and he recited Surah Ta-Ha up to His saying: ﴿Has there come to you the story of Musa (Moses)?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 9]. Then the Najashi wept, and so did his people who had come as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who were seventy men, when he recited to them Surah Ya-Sin, and they wept. ﴿Overflowing with tears﴾: they become filled with tears until they overflow, because fayd (overflowing) is for a vessel, or other thing, to become full until what is in it spills out from its sides. So the overflowing, which is from fullness, is placed in the position of fullness; or the intensification is intended in describing them as weeping, so their eyes are made as though they overflow of themselves, i.e., they flow because of weeping. The "min" in ﴿mimma 'arafu﴾ ("because of what they recognized") indicates the starting point, meaning that the overflowing of tears began and arose from the recognition of the truth and was on account of it. The "min" in ﴿min al-haqq﴾ ("of the truth") is either explanatory of the relative clause "what they recognized," or partitive, meaning that they recognized some of the truth and it made them weep; so how much more so when they recognized all of it, recited the Qur'an, and comprehended the Sunnah! The phrase "yaqulun" ("they say") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the subject in "'arafu" (they recognized): ﴿Our Lord, we have believed﴾ in Muhammad ﷺ, and what is meant is the initiation of faith and entry into it. ﴿So write us down among the witnesses﴾, i.e., among the community of Muhammad ﷺ, who are witnesses over the rest of the nations on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. They said this because they found their mention in the Gospel as such.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 84:

﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we should not believe in God﴾: this is a rebuke and a remote-seeming denial of the absence of faith, despite the presence of what would necessitate it, namely the hope that God would bestow His favour upon them by [granting them] the companionship of the righteous. It is also said: when they returned to their people, they blamed them, and they answered them with this.

"Mā lanā" (what is with us) is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar), and "lā nu'minu" (that we should not believe) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: not believing, like your saying: "Mā laka qā'iman?" (what is with you standing?). ﴿And what has come to us﴾, and [what has come to us] ﴿of the truth﴾, meaning: Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. ﴿And we hope﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the agent in "nu'minu," and the implied sense is: while we hope ﴿that our Lord will admit us﴾ into the Garden ﴿along with the righteous people﴾, the prophets and the believers.

﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said﴾, i.e., for their saying ﴿"Our Lord, we believe"﴾ and their affirming it: ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; that is the reward of the good-doers﴾. In this is evidence that *iqrar* (verbal affirmation) is included in *iman* (faith), as is the view of the *fuqaha'* (jurists). The Karramiyya (a sect) held that faith is merely speech, relying on His saying: ﴿for what they said﴾. But the praise accompanied by the overflowing of tears in the context, and the excellence (*ihsan*) in the context, refutes that. And how can mere speech be faith, when Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]? He negated faith from them despite their saying "We believe in Allah," because there was no belief in the heart.

The people of *ma'rifa* (gnosis, mystical knowing) said: what is found in them consists of three things: weeping over estrangement, supplicating for bounty, and contentment with the decree. Whoever claims gnosis but does not possess these three is not truthful in his claim.

This is the commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 86:

﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ This is the consequence of rejection with regard to the enemies, and the first (verse) is the consequence of acceptance for the allies (awliya', the godly). It was revealed concerning a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, who swore that they would practise asceticism (tarahhub, withdrawal from worldly life), wear woollen garments (al-masuh), stand in prayer at night, fast by day, wander about the earth (yasihu), castrate their members (yajabbu madhakirahum), and not eat meat or fat (al-wadak), nor approach women or perfume.

﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾: that is, what is pleasant and delicious of the lawful. The meaning of "do not forbid" is: do not prohibit them to yourselves as though prohibiting them, or do not say, "We have made them unlawful for ourselves," out of excessive determination on your part to abandon them in asceticism and self-denial. (p-471) It was narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to eat chicken and faluda, and that sweets and honey pleased him. He also said: "Indeed the believer is sweet and loves sweetness." It is related from al-Hasan that he was invited to a meal, and with him were Farqad al-Sinji and his companions. They sat at the table, on which were various dishes of fattened chicken, faluda and other things. Farqad withdrew to one side, so al-Hasan asked: "Is he fasting?" They said: "No, but he dislikes these dishes." So al-Hasan turned to him and said: "O Furayqid, do you think that a Muslim would find fault with honey-flavored finest wheat flour with pure clarified butter?" Also from him: it was said to him, "So-and-so does not eat faluda, and says, 'I cannot render its thanks.'" He said: "Does he drink cold water?" They said: "Yes." He said: "He is ignorant, for Allah's blessing upon him in cold water is greater than His blessing upon him in faluda." ﴿And do not transgress﴾: do not exceed the limit that has been set for you in declaring something lawful or unlawful; or, do not overstep the bounds of what is lawful for you to what is forbidden for you; or, do not be extravagant in consuming the good things. ﴿Indeed Allah does not love the transgressors﴾ of His limits.

Translation of the passage:

﴿And eat of what God has provided for you, lawful and good.﴾ "Lawful and good" (ḥalālan ṭayyiban) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) relating to "what God has provided for you." ﴿And fear God﴾ is an emphasis (tawkīd) on the injunction contained in what He commanded. He reinforced it further with His words: ﴿in whom you believe﴾, because belief in Him necessitates taqwā (God-consciousness, piety) regarding what He has commanded and forbidden.

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths.﴾ *Laghw* (idle or unintended speech) in an oath is what falls away and carries no legal ruling. It is swearing to something one believes to be so when it is not as one thought. They had sworn to forbid the good things on the assumption that this was an act of devotion. When the verse was revealed, they said, "What then of our oaths?" So the following was revealed: ﴿But He will hold you accountable for the oaths you have bound with intent﴾, that is, for your binding of oaths, which means confirming them. (p-٤٧٢) The reading with the lightened form (*al-takhfif*) is that of the Kufans other than Hafs. *Al-'aqd* (binding) is resolve to engage in intercourse, and this cannot be conceived of regarding the past, so there is no expiation for a *ghamus* (perjurious oath about a past matter). According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, *al-'aqd* is the intention of the heart, and the perjurious oath is intended, so it is a binding oath, and thus expiation for it is prescribed. The meaning is: "But He will hold you accountable for what you have bound when you break them," so the time of the accountability is omitted because it was known to them. Or it means "for breaking what you have bound," so the genitive noun is omitted. ﴿Then its expiation﴾, that is, the expiation for breaking it, or the expiation for a bound oath. *Kaffara* (expiation) is an act that by its nature covers over a sin, that is, conceals it. ﴿Is feeding ten needy persons﴾. This means providing them with lunch and dinner, or it may be giving them food by way of transferring ownership, and for each person this is half a *sa'* (a dry measure) of wheat, or a *sa'* of barley, or a *sa'* of dates. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, it is one *mudd* (a smaller measure) for each needy person. ﴿From the average of what you feed your families﴾, that is, lunch and dinner, of wheat, since it is the more generous: three times with condiment; the least is once with dates or barley. ﴿Or clothing them﴾ is coordinated with "feeding," or with the position of ﴿from the average﴾. Its rationale is that ﴿from the average﴾ is an apposition to "feeding," and the apposition is what is intended in the speech. It is a garment that covers the nakedness. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is a waist-wrap, or a shirt, or a cloak. ﴿Or freeing a slave﴾, a believing or unbelieving one, since the text is unrestricted. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, made belief a condition, applying the unrestricted to the restricted in the expiation for killing. The meaning of "or" is choice, and the obligation of one of the three expiations. ﴿Whoever does not find﴾ any of them, ﴿then fasting for three days﴾ in succession, in accordance with the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud in this way. ﴿That﴾ mentioned, (p-٤٧٣) ﴿is the expiation of your oaths when you swear﴾ and break them. The mention of breaking is omitted because it is known that expiation is not obligatory by the oath itself, and for this reason it is not permitted to expiate before breaking the oath. ﴿And guard your oaths﴾, so keep them, and do not break them when breaking is not better; or, do not swear at all. (p-٤٧٣) ﴿Thus﴾, like that explanation, ﴿Allah makes clear His verses for you﴾, the signs of His law and His rulings, ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾ for His favor in what He teaches you and eases for you as a way out of it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 90:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan. So avoid it that you may be successful.﴾

﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إنَّما الخَمْرُ والمَيْسِرُ﴾ means: al-maysir (gambling, i.e., games of chance) ﴿والأنْصابُ﴾ means: al-ansab (idols), because they are set up (تُنْصَبُ) and worshipped ﴿والأزْلامُ﴾, which are the arrows (al-qidah) mentioned earlier ﴿رِجْسٌ﴾ means: impure (najas), or foul and loathsome (khabith mustaqdhar) ﴿مِن عَمَلِ الشَيْطانِ﴾ because it drives one to it, so it is as if it were his work. The pronoun in ﴿فاجْتَنِبُوهُ﴾ refers to al-rijs, or to the work of Satan, or to what has been mentioned, or to a omitted noun that is implied, as if it were said: "Indulging in intoxicants and gambling is..." and for this reason he said "rijs" (defilement). ﴿لَعَلَّكم تُفْلِحُونَ﴾ He emphasized the prohibition of intoxicants and gambling in several ways: by beginning the sentence with *innama* (indeed, only), by joining them with the worship of idols, and in the hadith: "The drinker of intoxicants is like the worshipper of an idol," and by making them defilement from the work of Satan, from whom nothing comes but pure evil; he commanded avoidance and made avoidance a part of success. And if avoidance is success, then engaging in it is loss.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 91:

﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer.﴾ He mentions the harm that results from them, namely the occurrence of mutual hostility and hatred among the companions of wine and gambling, and what they lead to of turning away from the remembrance of Allah and from observing the times of the prayer. He singled out the prayer from among the remembrance (of Allah) to increase its rank, as if he said: "and from the prayer in particular." He grouped wine and gambling together with the idols (ansab) and the arrow-divining stones (azlam) at the beginning, then mentioned them separately at the end, because the address is to the believers. He forbade them from what they used to indulge in, namely drinking wine and playing at gambling, and mentioned the idols and the arrow-divining stones in order to emphasize the prohibition of wine and gambling, and to show that all of these are among the practices of the people of polytheism. It is as if there is no distinction between the worshipper of an idol, the drinker of wine and the gambler. Then he mentioned the two separately so that it would be known that they are the intended subject of the mention. ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ This is among the most forceful ways of urging abstention, as if it were said: "What is in them of deterrents and warnings has been recited to you. Will you, with these deterrents, desist, or will you remain as you were, as if you had not been admonished and restrained?!"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 92:

﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware.﴾ "And be cautious and humble (khushu')," because when they are cautious, caution leads them to guard against every evil deed and to perform every good deed. ﴿But if you turn away﴾ from that, ﴿then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ — that is: know that by your turning away you have not harmed the Messenger, because he was only charged with the clear conveyance of the verses, and you have only harmed yourselves when you turned away from what you were charged with.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 93:

It was revealed concerning those who indulged in some of the wine (khamr) and gambling (maysir) before their prohibition: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾, i.e., what they drank of the wine and ate of the gains of gambling before their prohibition, ﴿when they fear God﴾ [from associating partners with Him] ﴿and believe﴾ in God ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ after belief, ﴿then fear God﴾ [from] wine and gambling after their prohibition ﴿and believe﴾ in their prohibition.

﴿Then fear God﴾ [from] all the other forbidden things. Or the first is [fearing God] from polytheism, the second [fearing God] from forbidden things, and the third [fearing God] from doubtful matters (shubuhat). ﴿And do good﴾ to people. ﴿And God loves the good-doers﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 94:

When Allah tested them with game in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, while they were in the state of ihram (iḥrām, the sacred state of pilgrimage), and it was abundant among them, so that it would come upon them in their camps and they could easily catch it with their hands and spear it with their lances, the following was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your lances can reach﴾. The meaning of yabluw (to test, to try) is "yakhtabiru" (to examine). It is, from Allah, for the purpose of making manifest what He knows of the servant, in accordance with what He knows, not for the sake of knowing what He did not know. And "min" (from) is for partition (tab'id), since not every game is forbidden, or it is for explaining the kind (bayan al-jins). ﴿That Allah may make evident who fears Him in the unseen﴾: that Allah may make manifest the existence of the fear of the one who fears Him by abstaining from hunting (p-475), just as He knew before its existence that it would exist, in order to reward him for his deed, not for His knowledge of it. ﴿So whoever transgresses﴾ by hunting ﴿after that﴾ test ﴿for him there is a painful punishment﴾. He diminished it in His saying: ﴿with something of the game﴾, so that it would be known that it is not among the great trials. And "tanaluhu" (which your hands can reach) is an attribute of "shay'" (something).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 95:**

﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game﴾, i.e., the hunted animal (*al-maṣīd*), since killing applies only to it. ﴿while you are in the state of iḥrām﴾, i.e., *muḥrimūn*, the plural of *ḥarām*, like *ruduḥ* as the plural of *raddāḥ*. It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the subject pronoun in "do not kill." ﴿And whoever of you kills it intentionally﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject pronoun, meaning: remembering that he is in iḥrām, or knowing that what he kills is something whose killing is forbidden to him. If he kills it forgetting his iḥrām, or shoots at game while thinking it is not game, then he is one who erred (*mukhṭi'*). The verse made intention a condition, even though the prohibitions of iḥrām are equal regarding intention and error, because the occasion of the revelation concerns one who acted intentionally. It is related that during the 'Umrah of al-Ḥudaybiyya a wild donkey appeared to them, and Abu al-Yusr charged at it and killed it. It was said to him, "You killed game while you are in iḥrām," and then the verse was revealed. Also, the basic case is the action of the intentional one, and the mistaken one is attached to it for severity. It is related from al-Zuhri: "The Book came down concerning intention, and the Sunnah came concerning error."

﴿then a penalty equal to what he killed﴾ (*fa-jazā'un mithlu mā qatala*), a reading of the Kufans. That is, upon him is a penalty that matches what he killed of game, and it is the value of the game, assessed at the place where it was hunted. If its value reaches the price of a sacrificial animal (*hady*), he is given the choice between sacrificing from the livestock an animal whose value equals the value of the game, or buying food with its value and giving each poor person half a *ṣā'* of wheat, or one *ṣā'* of other food. If he wishes, he may fast one day for the food of each poor person. According to Muhammad (al-Shaybani) and al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on them both, the "equal" is its counterpart from the livestock. If no livestock counterpart exists for it, then it is as has passed. The reading *fa-jazā'u mithli* with the genitive (through *iḍāfa*, construct phrase) is that of the others. Its original form was *fa-jazā'un mithla mā qatala*, meaning: upon him is that he must repay an equivalent of what he killed; then it was made a construct phrase, as you say: "I was amazed at the striking of Zayd, then at the striking of Zayd."

﴿from the livestock﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *qatala*, since what is killed is from the livestock, or an adjective (*ṣifa*) of *jazā'un*. ﴿judged by it﴾: by an equivalent of what he killed, ﴿two just men from among you﴾: two upright judges from among the Muslims. In this there is evidence that "equivalent" means value, because assessment requires reflection and effort, unlike visible things. Also, the unqualified "equivalent" in the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus (*ijmā'*) is restricted by form and meaning, or by meaning without form, or by form without meaning. Value is intended where there is no equivalent in form, by consensus, so no other meaning remains intended, since there is no generality in a shared term (*al-mushtarak*). If you say that His saying ﴿from the livestock﴾ contradicts interpreting "equivalent" as value, I reply: whoever makes value obligatory is given the choice to buy with it a sacrificial animal, or food, or to fast, as God Most High gave the choice in the verse. So "from the livestock" is an explanation of the sacrificial animal bought with the value, in one of the forms of choice, because whoever assesses the game and buys with its value a sacrificial animal and sacrifices it, has indeed repaid with an equivalent of what he killed from the livestock. Furthermore, the choice in the verse between repaying with the sacrificial animal, or expiating with food, or with fasting, is valid only if one assesses and, after assessment, considers which of the three to choose. But if he aims directly at the counterpart and makes it the sole obligation without choice, then when there is no counterpart, it is assessed at that time, and then he is given the choice between food and fasting. This contradicts what is in the verse. Do you not see His saying: ﴿or an expiation: feeding the poor, or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾, how He gave the choice among the three things, and there is no way to do that except by assessment?

﴿as a sacrificial animal﴾ (*hadyan*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *bihi*, meaning: he judges by it while it is a sacrificial animal. ﴿reaching the Kaaba﴾ is an adjective of *hadyan*, because its construct is not a true construct (*ghayr ḥaqīqiyya*). The meaning of its reaching the Kaaba is that it is slaughtered within the Sacred Precinct (*Ḥaram*). As for giving it in charity, it may be wherever you wish. According to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, it must be in the Ḥaram.

﴿or an expiation﴾ is coordinated with *jazā'un*. ﴿food﴾ is either an apposition (*badal*) of *kaffāra*, or the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), meaning: it is food. ﴿or an expiation of food﴾ with the construct, a reading of the Madinans and the Syrians. This construct is for specifying the first term, as if it were said: "or an expiation from food for the poor," as you say "a ring of silver," meaning "a ring made of silver."

﴿or its equivalent﴾ (*'adl*). It is also read with a kasra on the 'ayn (*'idl*). Al-Farra' said: *'adl* is what equals a thing of a different kind, like fasting and feeding, while *'idl* is its like of the same kind, as in the two loads (*'idlā al-ḥaml*). It is said: "I have a boy equal to your boy" with a kasra, when he is of the same kind. If it is meant that its value is like its value, but it is not of the same kind, one says: "he is the equal (*'adl*) of your boy" with a fatḥa.

﴿that﴾ refers to the food. ﴿fasting﴾ is a specification (*tamyīz*), like "I have its like, a man." The choice in this belongs to the killer. According to Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, the choice belongs to the two judges.

﴿so that he may taste the consequence of his deed﴾ is connected to the saying ﴿then a penalty﴾, meaning: upon him is that he must repay, or expiate, so that he may taste the evil of the consequence of violating the sanctity of iḥrām. The *wabāl* is what is disliked, and the harm that is suffered in the end from an evil deed because of its heaviness upon him. It derives from His saying: ﴿So We seized him with a heavy seizure﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:16], meaning: heavy and severe. A *ṭa'ām wabīl* is food that lies heavily upon the stomach and is not digested easily.

﴿God has pardoned what has passed﴾, for you, of game before the prohibition. ﴿But whoever returns﴾ to killing game after the prohibition, or during that iḥrām, ﴿God will take retribution from him﴾ through the penalty. It is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "so he, God will take retribution from him." ﴿And God is Almighty﴾, by imposing the rulings.

﴿Owner of retribution﴾ against whoever transgresses the limits of Islam.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 96:

﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾: the catches of the sea (ṣaydu l-baḥr), whether edible or not.

﴿and its food﴾: what is fed upon from its game. The meaning: it is lawful for you to benefit from everything that is hunted in the sea, and lawful for you to eat what is edible from it, which is fish alone.

﴿as a provision for you﴾: a maf'ul la-hu (object of purpose), i.e., it is lawful for you as a means of enjoyment for you ﴿and for the travellers﴾, that is, for the wayfarers. The meaning: its food is lawful for you as a means of enjoyment; for residents, who eat it fresh (ṭariyyan), and for your travellers, who take it along provisioned as dried fish (qadīdan), just as Musa (peace be upon him) took the fish with him on his journey to al-Khadir.

﴿But forbidden to you is the game of the land﴾: that which is hunted on land. This is what breeds on land, even if it lives in water at certain times, such as the duck; for it is seen as land game, because it is born on land, while the sea is its pasture, just as the sea is a trading ground for people. ﴿So long as you are in the state of ihram﴾: those in iḥrām. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in hunting within the Sacred Precinct (al-ḥaram), or in the state of iḥrām, ﴿to whom you will be gathered﴾: you will be raised, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

(p-478) ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah﴾, i.e., He made, ﴿the Sacred House﴾ a substitute (badal) or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan). ﴿Qiyaman﴾ is the second object. Or "made" is taken in the sense of "created," and qiyaman is a circumstantial accusative (hal). ﴿For the people﴾, i.e., a means of uplifting them (intiʿash) in the affairs of their religion, and a means of rising toward their aims in their livelihood and their hereafter, because of what is accomplished for them through their pilgrimage (hajj) and their lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah), and the various kinds of their benefits. It has been said: if they left it for a year, they would not be given respite and would not be delayed.

﴿And the Sacred Month﴾: the month in which the pilgrimage is performed, which is Dhu'l-Hijjah, because its being singled out from among the months for the holding of the season of the pilgrimage is a matter that Allah knows. Or it is meant to denote the class of the sacred months, which are: Rajab, Dhu'l-Qa'dah, Dhu'l-Hijjah, and Muharram.

﴿And the offerings﴾: what is brought as offerings to Makkah. ﴿And the garlands﴾: and what is garlanded from among them in particular, namely the camels (budn), for the reward in them is greater and the splendor of the pilgrimage is more manifest with them.

﴿That﴾: a reference either to the making of the Ka'bah a means of standing (qiyam), or to what was mentioned of preserving the sanctity of the state of ihram by abstaining from hunting and other things. ﴿So that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and that Allah is Knower of all things﴾: i.e., so that you may know that Allah knows the interests (maslahih) of what is in the heavens and what is in the earth. And how could He not know, when He is ʿAlim of all things?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 98:

﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for those who treat the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and the state of ihram lightly, ﴿and that Allah is Forgiving﴾ of the sins of those who honor the great sacred rites (al-mash'ir al-'izam), ﴿Merciful﴾ toward the offender who seeks refuge in the Sacred City (al-balad al-haram).

The Messenger has no duty but to convey (the message). This is an emphatic statement of the obligation to carry out what one has been commanded, and that the Messenger has already discharged what was incumbent upon him of conveying (the message), the proof has been established against you, and obedience has become binding upon you, so there is no excuse for you in neglect. "And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal," so your hypocrisy and your agreement (with the truth) are not hidden from Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 100:

﴿Say: The corrupt and the good are not equal⁠—﴾ When He informed that He knows what they reveal and what they conceal, He mentioned that their corrupt and their good are not equal; rather He distinguishes between them, so He punishes the corrupt, i.e., the disbeliever, and rewards the good, i.e., the Muslim. ﴿Even if the abundance of the corrupt impresses you, so be wary of Allah﴾, and prefer the good, even if little, over the corrupt, even if abundant. It has been said: this is general, covering lawful and unlawful wealth, righteous and wicked deeds, and good and bad people. ﴿O people of understanding⁠—﴾ i.e., of pure intellects ﴿so that you may prosper.﴾

They used to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) about things as a test, so this was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things﴾. Al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi), Sibawayh, and the majority of the Basran grammarians said: its original form was shay'a'' with two hamzas between which there is an alif. It is of the pattern fa'lā' derived from the word shay', and its second hamza is for the feminine marker; for this reason it is not declined, like ḥamrā' (the feminine of ḥamr). It is singular in form but plural in meaning. When the two adjacent hamzas were found heavy, the first one, which is the lam of the root (the final radical), was moved forward and placed before the shīn, so its pattern became la fā'ā'. The conditional clause and the clause coordinated with it, namely His saying: ﴿If they are shown to you, they will distress you; and if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be shown to you﴾, are a description of "things" (ashyā'). That is: if you ask about these difficult obligations during the time of revelation, while the Messenger is among you, those obligations will be made apparent to you, which will distress you, that is, grieve you and weigh heavily upon you, for you will be commanded to bear them, and so you will expose yourselves to the wrath of Allah by neglecting them. ﴿Allah has pardoned you concerning them﴾: Allah has pardoned you for what preceded of your questioning, so do not return to the like of it. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾: He does not punish you except after warning.

The pronoun in ﴿قَدْ سَألَها﴾ ("Indeed, a people before you asked it") does not refer back to "things" (ashya') in a way that would require it to be governed by the preposition "ʿan"; rather it refers to the question (al-masʾalah) that is indicated by "لا تَسْألُوا" ("Do not ask"). That is: a people from among the earlier generations asked this very question, ﴿ثُمَّ أصْبَحُوا بِها﴾ "then they became, because of it, ﴿كافِرِينَ﴾ disbelievers," as is known concerning the Children of Israel.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 103:

﴿Allah has not instituted any bahira, sa'iba, wasila, or ham.﴾ The people of the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance, i.e., the pre-Islamic period) used to do the following: when a she-camel gave birth to five offspring, the last of which was a male, they would slit her ear (baharu udhunaha, i.e., they split it, from bahr, to slit the ear) and abstain from riding her and from slaughtering her, and she was not to be driven away from water or pasture. She was called the bahira. A man would also say: "If I return from my journey, or recover from my illness, then my she-camel is a sa'iba (one set free)," and he would make her like the bahira in forbidding any benefit from her. It was also said: when a man freed a slave, he would say, "He is a sa'iba," so there would be no blood-money (aql) or inheritance between them. And when a ewe gave birth to seven offspring, if the seventh was a male, the men would eat it; if it was a female, it was let loose among the sheep; and likewise if it was a male and a female together. They said: "She has joined (wassalat) her brother," so the wasila is in the sense of the wasila (the one joined). And when a stallion's offspring from his loins reached ten, they said: "His back has been protected (qad hamiya zahruhu)," so he would not be ridden, nor carried upon, nor prevented from water or pasture.

The meaning of ﴿ma ja'ala﴾ ("has not instituted") is: He did not legislate that, nor command it. ﴿But those who disbelieve﴾, by their forbidding what they forbade, ﴿invent lies against Allah﴾ in attributing this prohibition to Him. ﴿And most of them do not reason﴾ that Allah did not prohibit that; and they are their common folk.

﴿وَإذا قِيلَ لَهم تَعالَوْا إلى ما أنْـزَلَ اللهُ وإلى الرَسُولِ﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them: "Come to what Allah has sent down, and to the Messenger."﴾ That is: "Hasten (halumma) to the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, that these things are not forbidden." ﴿قالُوا حَسْبُنا ما وجَدْنا عَلَيْهِ آباءَنا﴾ ﴿They say: "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon."﴾ That is: what we found them upon suffices us. "Hasbuna" (حسبنا) is a mubtada' (subject), and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿ما وجَدْنا﴾, where "ma" (ما) is in the sense of "alladhi" (الَّذِي, "that which"). The waw in ﴿أوَلَوْ كانَ آباؤُهُمْ﴾ ﴿Even though their fathers...﴾ is for the situational sense (lil-hal), and the interrogative hamzah of denial (hamzat al-inkar) has entered upon it, and its implied construction is: "Is it sufficient for them that that is so, even though their fathers..." ﴿لا يَعْلَمُونَ شَيْئًا ولا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ ﴿knew nothing and were not guided.﴾ That is: taqlid (imitation, blind following) is valid only with one who has knowledge and is guided. His being guided is known only through proof (hujjah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 105:

﴿O you who have believed, take charge of your own selves; the one who is astray cannot harm you once you are guided.﴾ The word ﴿أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ (anfusakum, "your selves") is in the accusative case, governed by ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (alaykum, "upon you"). The latter is one of the "names of verbs" (asma' al-af'al), meaning: "Keep to (lazimu) the reform of your selves." The kaf and mim in ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ are in the genitive position, because the active participle here is the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur) as a whole, not "ʿalā" alone.

﴿لا يَضُرُّكُمْ﴾ (la yadurrukum, "it will not harm you") is in the nominative case, as a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf), or it is in the jussive case as a response to the imperative (jawab al-amr). The raʼ is vowelled with a damma only in order to harmonise with the damma of the ḍād (ittiba' li-dammat al-ḍad).

﴿مَن ضَلَّ إذا اهْتَدَيْتُمْ﴾ (man ḍalla idha ihtadaytum, "the one who is astray, once you are guided"): the believers' selves would be consumed by grief (ḥasrah) over the stubborn disbelievers, wishing that they would enter Islam. So it was said to them: ﴿عَلَيْكم أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ ("take charge of your own selves"), and [it is the reform of them] for which you are held responsible. ﴿لا يَضُرُّكُمْ﴾ ("it will not harm you") — the straying of others from your religion — if you are rightly guided. The intended meaning is not the abandonment of enjoining good and forbidding evil, for abandoning them while able to do so is not permissible. ﴿إلى اللهِ مَرْجِعُكم جَمِيعًا﴾ ("to God is your return, all of you"): your return. ﴿فَيُنَبِّئُكم بِما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("then He will inform you of what you used to do"), then He will recompense you for your deeds.

It is narrated that Badil, the freed slave (mawla) of Amr ibn al-As, who was among the emigrants (al-Muhajirun, those who migrated with the Prophet (ﷺ) from Makkah to Madinah), set out for Syria with Adi and Tamim, who were both Christians. Badil fell ill, and he wrote a document listing what he had with him, put it among his belongings, and did not tell his two companions about it. He instructed them to deliver his belongings to his family, and then he died. They searched his belongings and took a silver vessel. Then the people of Badil found the document and demanded the vessel from them, but they denied having it. So they brought the two men before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, let there be a testimony between you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest: two...﴾. The word "ithnan" (two) is in the nominative case because it is the khabar (predicate) of the mubtada' (subject), which is "shahadah" (testimony), with the implied meaning "the testimony among you is the testimony of two"; or because it is the fa'il (agent) of "shahadah baynikum", meaning: in what has been prescribed for you, two should bear witness. The word "bayn" (between) has been used in an extended sense, so the verbal noun is attached to it. ﴿When death approaches﴾ is an adverbial clause (zarf) modifying the testimony. ﴿At the time of bequest﴾ is a substitute (badal) for it. In this substitution there is evidence that the bequest is obligatory, because the approach of death is among the things that will certainly occur. And ﴿at the time of bequest﴾ being a substitute indicates that the bequest exists; if it existed without choice, the trial would be void, so it was transferred to the obligatory sense. "Approach of death" means its imminence and the appearance of signs that the term has come.

﴿Two just men﴾ is an attribute of "two", ﴿from among you﴾, meaning from your relatives, because they know the state of the deceased best. ﴿Or two others﴾ is coordinated with "two", ﴿from other than you﴾, meaning from strangers. ﴿If you travel through the land﴾ means if you journey in it. "You" (antum) is the agent of a verb implied by the apparent verb that follows it: ﴿if the calamity of death strikes you﴾. Or "from among you" means from among the Muslims, and "from other than you" means from among the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimmah, non-Muslim protected subjects). It has been said that this ruling is abrogated (mansukh, i.e., superseded by a later ruling), since the testimony of a dhimmi against a Muslim is not valid, and it was permitted only at the beginning of Islam because Muslims were few. ﴿You detain them﴾ means you hold them back (taqifunahuma) for the oath. This is a new sentence, or it is an attribute of the saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾, meaning: ﴿or two others from other than you﴾ who are detained. The parenthetical clause ﴿if you travel through the land and the calamity of death strikes you﴾ comes between the attribute and the thing it describes.

﴿After the prayer﴾ means after the Asr prayer, because it is the time when people gather. It is narrated from al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, that it was after Asr or after Zuhr, because the people of the Hijaz used to sit for judgment after these two. In the hadith of Badil: when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed the Asr prayer and called Adi and Tamim, and made them swear an oath at the minbar (pulpit). They swore, and then the vessel was found in Makkah. The people said: "We bought it from Tamim and Adi." ﴿Then they shall swear by Allah﴾, meaning they shall take an oath by Him, ﴿if you doubt them﴾, meaning if you have suspicion regarding their trustworthiness. This is a parenthetical clause between "they shall swear" and its answer, which is ﴿we will not sell﴾. The answer of the conditional is omitted, its meaning being sufficient for it. The implied sense is: ﴿if you doubt them﴾ concerning their case, then make them swear ﴿by Him﴾, by Allah, or by the oath. ﴿For any price﴾ means for any compensation from worldly goods. ﴿Even if it be a near kinsman﴾, meaning, even if the one for whom we swear is one of our kin. That is: we will not swear falsely by Allah for the sake of wealth, even if the one for whom we swear is close to us. ﴿Nor do we conceal the testimony of Allah﴾, meaning the testimony that Allah commanded to be preserved and honored. ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the sinners﴾, if we concealed it. It has been said: if by "the two" are meant the witnesses, then the oath for the two witnesses has been abrogated; but if by them are meant the two executors (wasiyyan), then their oath has not been abrogated.

ﷺ-free passage; translating faithfully.
